modules.title: Your Financial Starting Point
modules.summary: Before you build a budget, you need an honest picture of where your money stands today. This module helps you capture that picture calmly, in one place.

lessons.title: Know Your Starting Point
lessons.summary: Learn the six areas you need to see before any budget can work.

sections.what: A quick inventory of the six areas that make up your financial picture: income, regular expenses, debt, savings, major upcoming expenses and goals.
sections.why: A budget built on guesses breaks quickly. Knowing your starting point means every later decision rests on real numbers instead of hope.
sections.do: List what you already know in each of the six areas, using rough numbers where exact ones are not to hand.
sections.output: A rough first list of your six money areas

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Most budgets fail for a simple reason: they start with a plan instead of a picture. People write down what they *want* to spend before they know what they *do* spend. This system works the other way around.

**Visibility → Planning → Control → Review.** Visibility comes first.

Before building anything, you look at six areas:

1. **Current income** – everything that comes in, from every source.
2. **Regular expenses** – the bills and costs that repeat.
3. **Debt** – what you owe and to whom.
4. **Savings** – money already set aside, wherever it sits.
5. **Major upcoming expenses** – known costs in the next 12 months, such as a renewal, a celebration or school fees.
6. **Financial goals** – what you want your money to do for you.

You do not need exact figures yet. A rough number you can see is more useful than a perfect number you never write down. You will refine every area in later modules.

A few things that help:

- **Use your own records.** Bank statements, payslips and app histories are better than memory.
- **Write "unknown" where you genuinely don't know.** That is useful information, not a failure.
- **Keep it private and neutral.** This is a starting point, not a score.

All amounts in this course are in your currency. Examples use round numbers so the method is easy to follow; they are not recommendations.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Sam opens a notes app and spends ten minutes on the six areas:

- Income: salary of about 20,000 a month, plus occasional freelance work, amount unknown.
- Regular expenses: rent 7,000, phone 500, transport roughly 1,500.
- Debt: a store account (balance unknown) and a car loan of about 60,000.
- Savings: 3,000 in a savings account.
- Upcoming expenses: car service in March, a wedding gift in June.
- Goals: "stop feeling surprised at month-end."

It is incomplete, and that is fine. Sam now knows exactly which three numbers to look up.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Set a 10-minute timer. On paper or in a note, write the six headings: Income, Regular expenses, Debt, Savings, Upcoming expenses, Goals.

Under each heading, write whatever you know right now. Use round numbers. Where you are unsure, write "check" next to the item.

When the timer ends, circle every "check" item. Those are your look-ups for this week. Then open the Financial Snapshot and enter anything you are already confident about. You will complete the rest in lesson 1.3.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
This week, gather the documents that turn your "check" items into real numbers: your latest payslip or income records, one or two recent bank statements, and the most recent statement for each debt.

Keep them in one folder, physical or digital. You will use the same folder throughout this course, so name it something you will find again, such as "2026 Money System".

questions.q: Why does this system start with a picture of your finances instead of a spending plan?
options: Because a plan built on guesses tends to break quickly
Because budgets should only cover income
Because exact numbers are required before you start
questions.explain: Visibility comes first. Planning works far better once you can see real income, expenses, debt and savings.

sections.markdown:
- You know the six areas of your financial picture.
- You have a rough first list, with gaps marked "check".
- You know which documents to gather this week.

lessons.title: Net Position
lessons.summary: Record what you own and what you owe at a high level, without judgment.

sections.what: Your net position is a high-level comparison of what you own (assets) against what you owe (liabilities).
sections.why: It gives you one reference point you can revisit later to see whether things are moving in the direction you want.
sections.do: List your main assets and liabilities with approximate values, then subtract liabilities from assets.
sections.output: Your net position, recorded once as a baseline

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Your **net position** is a simple calculation:

**What you own − what you owe = net position**

**Assets** are things with money value that you own. At a high level this might include:

- Cash and bank balances
- Savings accounts
- Retirement or investment accounts (use the latest statement value)
- A vehicle (an estimated resale value, not what you paid)
- Property, if you own any (a cautious estimate)

**Liabilities** are amounts you owe:

- Credit cards and store accounts
- Personal loans
- Vehicle finance
- Home loans
- Money owed to family or friends

Keep it high level. You do not need to value every item in your home. Five to ten lines are usually enough.

> This is a snapshot, not a judgment.

Many people have a negative net position at some stage, especially early in their working life, while studying, or after a large purchase. A negative number simply tells you where you are starting. What matters for this course is that you can *see* it, so you can plan from it.

Record the date next to your figure. Net position changes as balances, values and debts change, so a dated snapshot lets you compare like with like when you check again later, for example every quarter. Use estimates you can explain, and stay consistent each time.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Lindiwe lists her position in round numbers:

- Assets: bank account 4,000; savings 10,000; car (estimated resale) 80,000. Total 94,000.
- Liabilities: car finance 70,000; credit card 12,000; store account 3,000. Total 85,000.

94,000 − 85,000 = a net position of 9,000.

She writes the date beside it. She does not need to decide yet whether it is "good". She now has a fixed point to compare against when she checks again in three months.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Financial Snapshot and find the assets and liabilities fields.

1. Add each asset as a short line with an approximate value, for example "Savings account – 5,000".
2. Add each liability the same way, using the latest balance you have.
3. Add up each list and enter the totals.
4. Subtract total liabilities from total assets and record the result with today's date.

If a value is uncertain, use a cautious estimate and note it.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Put a reminder in your calendar three months from today titled "Net position check". When it comes up, repeat the same calculation using the same method and compare the two figures.

If you share finances with a partner, decide together whether you track one combined position or separate ones. Either can work; consistency matters more than the choice.

questions.q: Lindiwe has assets of 94,000 and liabilities of 85,000. What is her net position?
questions.explain: Net position is assets minus liabilities: 94,000 − 85,000 = 9,000.

questions.q: What is the best way to treat a negative net position?
options: As proof that budgeting won't work
As a starting point to plan from
As a reason to stop tracking
questions.explain: The snapshot is information, not a verdict. It shows where planning begins.

sections.markdown:
- You listed your main assets and liabilities.
- You calculated and dated your net position.
- You set a reminder to compare it again later.

lessons.title: Financial Snapshot
lessons.summary: Bring your numbers together into one page: the Financial Snapshot.

sections.what: The Financial Snapshot is a one-page summary of your monthly income, fixed and variable spending, debt, savings, upcoming large expenses and goals.
sections.why: Every later module builds on it. It also shows you, often for the first time, how your monthly money actually flows.
sections.do: Complete every field of the Financial Snapshot using the documents you gathered.
sections.output: A completed Financial Snapshot

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
The Financial Snapshot pulls everything from the last two lessons into one page. It covers:

- **Monthly income** – your typical take-home amount after deductions.
- **Monthly fixed expenses** – costs that are roughly the same each month, like rent, insurance and subscriptions.
- **Typical variable spending** – food, transport, personal and household spending. An estimate is fine here; Module 4 will show you the real figure.
- **Debt balances** – total owed, plus total monthly minimum payments.
- **Savings** – what you currently have set aside.
- **Upcoming large expenses** – known costs in the next 12 months.
- **Current goals** – written in plain words.

Once these are filled in, one quick calculation is very revealing:

**Monthly income − fixed expenses − variable spending − debt payments = what's left (or short)**

If the result is positive, you have room to plan. If it is negative, or close to zero, that is important information: it explains why money has felt tight. Either way, the next modules will help you look closer.

A few guidelines:

- **Use take-home income**, not the gross figure, unless you are self-employed and set tax aside separately. Tax rules differ by country, so check how they apply to you with an official or qualified source.
- **Round to sensible figures.** Precision comes later.
- **Mark estimates** so you know which numbers to confirm.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Thabo completes his snapshot:

- Monthly income: 25,000
- Fixed expenses: 11,000
- Variable spending (estimate): 8,000
- Debt: balances 40,000; monthly minimums 3,000
- Savings: 6,000
- Upcoming: car licence renewal, holiday in December
- Goals: build a reserve; pay down the credit card

25,000 − 11,000 − 8,000 − 3,000 = 3,000 left each month, on paper. Thabo notes that his savings haven't grown in months, so his variable estimate may be low. That becomes his focus for Module 4.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Financial Snapshot and complete every field. Work from the folder of documents you gathered in lesson 1.1.

Then do the calculation: income minus fixed expenses, variable spending and debt payments. Write the result in the "what's left" field.

Finally, answer the reflection question in your own words: what surprised you? One honest sentence is enough.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Keep your snapshot open while you work through the next five modules. Each one zooms into one line of it: income (Module 2), fixed expenses (Module 3), variable spending (Module 4), debt (Module 5) and savings (Module 6).

As your numbers become more accurate, come back and update the snapshot. By the end, the estimates should be replaced with real figures.

questions.q: Which income figure should most people use in the snapshot?
options: The highest month they have ever earned
Their income goal for next year
questions.explain: Take-home income is the money you actually have to work with each month. Use the typical amount, not the best month.

sections.markdown:
- Your Financial Snapshot is complete.
- You know roughly what is left, or short, each month.
- You marked the estimates you will confirm in later modules.
- **Output: Financial Snapshot.**

modules.title: Understand Your Income
modules.summary: Your budget can only be as reliable as your income picture. This module maps every source, when it arrives and how much it varies.
modules.outcome: Your Income System: Income Tracker + Income Calendar

lessons.title: Identify Every Income Source
lessons.summary: Find and list every source of money that comes in.

sections.what: A complete list of every legitimate source of income you receive, regular or occasional.
sections.why: Missing income makes your budget look worse than it is; overcounting makes it look better. Both lead to poor decisions.
sections.do: List each income source with its typical amount and whether it is steady or variable.
sections.output: A full list of your income sources

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Many people think of income as "my salary". In reality, money often arrives from several places. Common sources include:

- **Salary or wages** – regular employment income.
- **Freelance or contract work** – paid per project or per hour.
- **Business income** – what you actually take out of a business, not the business's total sales.
- **Side income** – selling items, tutoring, weekend work.
- **Commission or bonuses** – often variable and not guaranteed.
- **Benefits or other legitimate income** – grants, allowances, rental income, regular support from family, maintenance payments.

For each source, note two things:

1. **Typical amount** – what usually arrives, after deductions where they apply.
2. **Steady or variable** – does it arrive in the same amount each time?

**Business owners and freelancers:** separate business money from personal money where you can. For personal budgeting, the useful figure is what you pay yourself. Business taxes and contributions vary by country, so confirm your obligations with your tax authority or a qualified adviser.

**Irregular income still counts.** A once-a-year bonus or a few freelance jobs are real income. You will handle them carefully in lesson 2.3 so you don't spend money before it arrives.

The aim here is completeness. Small, occasional sources matter, because they often explain why the numbers never quite add up.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Aisha thought she had one income. Going through her bank statement, she finds four:

- Salary: 18,000 a month, steady.
- Weekend tutoring: 1,000 to 3,000 a month, variable.
- Selling handmade cards online: about 500 most months, variable.
- Annual bonus: possible but not guaranteed, usually in December.

Her real income picture is bigger than she thought, and less predictable. Both facts change how she plans.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open two months of bank statements. Highlight every deposit that is not a transfer between your own accounts.

Group them by source. For each one, add a row to the Income Tracker with the date, source and amount received. Leave "expected" blank for now if you are unsure; you will fill it in during the next lesson.

Ask yourself: is there any income that arrives in cash or to another account that the statements don't show? Add those too.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
For the rest of this week, log every income payment in the Income Tracker the day it arrives. It takes under a minute.

If you have a variable source, note anything that affected the amount in the Notes column, such as "fewer sessions, school holiday". Those notes will make your planning in lesson 2.3 much more realistic.

questions.q: For personal budgeting, what is the most useful income figure for a small business owner?
questions.explain: Business sales are not personal income. What you pay yourself is the money available for your personal budget.

sections.markdown:
- You found every income source, including small and occasional ones.
- Each source is marked steady or variable.
- Your income is starting to appear in the Income Tracker.

lessons.title: Income Timing
lessons.summary: Record when each income arrives, how often, and how much it varies.

sections.what: Income timing records the expected amount, date, frequency and variability of each income source.
sections.why: Bills are due on fixed dates. If you know when money lands, you can line up payments and avoid short gaps even when the monthly total is enough.
sections.do: For each income source, record expected amount, expected date, frequency and variability, then compare expected with actual.
sections.output: An Income Tracker showing expected versus actual income

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Knowing *how much* you earn is half the picture. The other half is *when*.

For each income source, record:

- **Source** – where it comes from.
- **Expected amount** – what you expect to receive.
- **Expected date** – the day it usually arrives.
- **Frequency** – weekly, every two weeks, monthly, per project, annually.
- **Variability** – steady, somewhat variable, or highly variable.

Timing matters because expenses don't wait. Rent might be due on the 1st, while your salary lands on the 25th and freelance payments arrive whenever clients pay. Even with enough money over a month, a poorly timed week can feel like a shortage.

**Expected versus actual** is where the Income Tracker becomes powerful. Each time money arrives, record what you expected and what you actually received. The tracker calculates the difference for you:

**Difference = actual − expected**

- A **positive** difference means more arrived than expected.
- A **negative** difference means less arrived, or it was late.
- Tick **Received?** only once the money is actually in your account.

Over a few months, the differences show you how reliable each source really is. A source that is regularly 20% below expectation needs a lower planning figure. A source that is always on time can be planned with more confidence.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Kofi records one month in his Income Tracker:

- 25th, Salary: expected 22,000, actual 22,000, received. Difference 0.
- 10th, Client A invoice: expected 5,000, actual 5,000, received.
- 20th, Client B invoice: expected 4,000, actual 0, not received. Note: "paying next month".

Total expected 31,000; actual 27,000; difference −4,000. Kofi now sees that client payments slip, so he decides to plan around salary first and treat client income as "spend once received".

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Income Tracker. For each income source you listed in lesson 2.1:

1. Enter the expected date and expected amount for this month.
2. In Notes, add the frequency and whether it is steady or variable.
3. For anything already received, enter the actual amount and tick Received?

Check the Difference column. Note any source with a gap and what caused it.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
At the end of this month, review the tracker. Ask:

- Which sources arrived as expected?
- Which were late or lower?
- Is there a gap between your income date and a large bill date?

If there is a timing gap, write down one possible fix, such as asking whether a due date can be moved, or setting money aside from the previous payment. Check any change with the provider directly.

questions.q: Expected income was 5,000 and actual income was 4,200. What does the Difference column show?
questions.explain: Difference = actual − expected = 4,200 − 5,000 = −800. A negative difference means less arrived than expected.

questions.q: Why does income timing matter if the monthly total covers your bills?
options: Bills have due dates that may come before the income arrives
questions.explain: Even with enough money over the month, a bill due before payday can create a short gap.

sections.markdown:
- You recorded amount, date, frequency and variability for each source.
- Your Income Tracker compares expected with actual.
- You can see which income is reliable and which is not.

lessons.title: Build an Income Calendar
lessons.summary: Map your expected income across every month of 2026.

sections.what: An Income Calendar places each expected income amount in the month it should arrive, from January to December 2026.
sections.why: Months are not all equal. Seeing income across the whole year shows the lean months, the bonus months and the gaps before they happen.
sections.do: Enter expected income for each source in each month of 2026, using conservative amounts for anything variable.
sections.output: A 2026 Income Calendar

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Your Income Tracker shows what happened. Your **Income Calendar** shows what you expect across the year.

For each month of 2026, list each source and the amount you expect. Steady income is simple: the same amount, every month. Variable and occasional income needs more care.

**Use conservative planning assumptions.** For variable income, do not assume your best month will repeat. Some practical approaches:

- **Use a lower-than-average figure.** Look at what you received over the past 6 to 12 months and plan with a figure near the lower end.
- **Plan only on guaranteed income** and treat everything else as extra when it arrives.
- **Leave bonuses out of the plan** until they are confirmed in writing.

The calendar has two amount columns:

- **Expected amount** – what you realistically think might arrive.
- **Planning amount** – the cautious figure you will actually budget with.

For steady income, these are usually the same. For variable income, the planning amount is lower. The gap between the two totals is a cushion: if a good month happens, that extra can go to savings, debt or sinking funds instead of quietly disappearing.

Also note known changes: a contract ending, a planned increase, parental leave, or a seasonal business slowdown. Put them in the months they affect.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Nomsa is a hairdresser whose income rises in December and dips in January. Her past 12 months ranged from 12,000 to 30,000, with most months near 18,000.

In her calendar she enters:

- Most months: expected 18,000, planning 15,000.
- January and February: expected 14,000, planning 12,000.
- November and December: expected 26,000, planning 20,000.

Her planning total for the year is lower than her expected total. She builds her monthly budget on the planning figures, so a slow month is no longer a crisis.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Income Calendar.

1. Add one row per income source per month, starting with your steady income for January to December 2026.
2. Add variable sources month by month, using what you know about busy and quiet periods.
3. Fill in a cautious planning amount for each row.
4. Add notes for any expected changes.

Compare the two totals at the bottom.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Look at your calendar and highlight your three lowest planning months. Those months need extra attention when you build your monthly budget in Module 9.

Each month, compare the Income Calendar with your Income Tracker. If a source consistently comes in lower than planned, lower its planning amount for the rest of the year.

questions.q: Which approach fits conservative planning for variable income?
options: Plan using a figure near the lower end of recent months
Ignore variable income completely, even after it arrives
Plan using next year's income goal
questions.explain: A cautious planning figure means slow months don't break your budget, and good months create a surplus you can direct on purpose.

sections.markdown:
- You mapped expected income across every month of 2026.
- Variable income has a cautious planning amount.
- You know your lowest income months in advance.
- **Output: Income Tracker + Income Calendar.**

modules.title: Fixed Expenses
modules.summary: Fixed expenses are the commitments that repeat whether you think about them or not. This module puts every one of them on a single tracker so nothing surprises you.

lessons.title: What Is Fixed?
lessons.summary: Learn what counts as a fixed expense and list yours.

sections.what: Fixed expenses are recurring costs that stay roughly the same amount and arrive on a predictable schedule.
sections.why: They are usually your biggest and most committed costs. Seeing them clearly shows how much of your income is already spoken for.
sections.do: List every fixed expense you pay, using bank statements and account records.
sections.output: A complete list of your fixed expenses

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A **fixed expense** has two features: the amount is roughly the same each time, and it repeats on a schedule. Common examples:

- **Rent or home loan repayment**
- **Insurance** – car, home contents, life, medical cover
- **Phone and internet**
- **Subscriptions** – streaming, music, cloud storage, apps, gym
- **Loan payments** – vehicle finance, personal loans, student loans
- **Regular transport commitments** – a monthly transport pass, lift club or school transport
- **Childcare or school fees** paid on a set schedule
- **Regular contributions** such as a debit order to a savings or retirement product

Not every fixed expense is monthly. Some are **weekly** (a lift club), **quarterly** (some insurance or levies) or **annual** (a vehicle licence, software renewals, a membership). Annual costs are the easiest to forget and the most likely to cause a surprise.

**Grey areas:** electricity, water and similar utilities can vary by season. If they change only a little, treat them as fixed using a typical amount. If they swing a lot, you can also track them in Module 4.

Where to look:

1. Bank statements – debit orders and recurring card payments.
2. Card statements – subscriptions often hide here.
3. Email – search for "renewal", "subscription" or "invoice".
4. App stores – your account lists active subscriptions.

Aim to find everything, even small amounts.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Pieter starts with what he remembers: rent, car payment, phone. That is three items.

After searching his bank statement and email, his list grows to eleven: rent, car payment, car insurance, phone, home internet, two streaming services, cloud storage, gym, an annual antivirus renewal and a quarterly security levy.

Four of those he had forgotten. None are wrong to have, but now they are visible.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your last two bank statements and your card statement. Mark every payment that repeats.

Add each one as a row in the Fixed Expense Tracker: name and amount. Don't worry about frequency or due dates yet; that is the next lesson.

Then search your email for "renewal" and "subscription" and add anything annual or quarterly you find.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
For the next week, whenever a debit order or recurring payment goes off, check it is on your tracker. If it isn't, add it.

Ask anyone you share costs with whether there are commitments you don't see, such as a policy in their name that you both rely on.

questions.q: Which of these is most likely a fixed expense?
questions.explain: An internet subscription is the same amount on a set schedule. The others vary week to week and are variable spending.

sections.markdown:
- You know what makes an expense fixed.
- You searched statements, email and app stores.
- Every fixed expense is listed on your tracker.

lessons.title: Review Recurring Commitments
lessons.summary: Add the detail to each commitment and decide which ones you still need.

sections.what: A review of each fixed expense: its amount, due date, frequency, payment method, whether it is necessary, and when you will next review it.
sections.why: Recurring costs often continue long after they stop being useful. A calm review puts each one back under your control.
sections.do: Complete every column of the Fixed Expense Tracker and mark each commitment necessary or not.
sections.output: A fully detailed Fixed Expense Tracker

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
For each fixed expense, record:

- **Amount** – what you pay each time.
- **Due date** – when it leaves your account, e.g. "1st of month" or "15 March".
- **Frequency** – weekly, monthly, quarterly or annual.
- **Payment method** – debit order, card, manual transfer, cash.
- **Necessary?** – is it essential to how you live or work right now?
- **Review date** – when you will check this commitment again.

**"Necessary" is your call, not a test.** A gym membership may be essential for one person and unused by another. Ask yourself:

- Do I actually use this?
- Would I sign up for it again today at this price?
- Is there a cheaper version that would do the job?

Unticking "necessary" does not mean you must cancel it. It means it is a candidate to review.

**Before changing anything,** check the terms. Some contracts have cancellation fees, notice periods or minimum terms. Insurance and loan agreements can have important conditions. Contact the provider, read your agreement, and where cover or legal obligations are involved, get guidance from the provider or a qualified adviser before cancelling.

**Review dates** keep this from being a one-off exercise. Set a date for each item, such as a month before an annual renewal or a contract end date, so you can compare options while you still have time to act.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Pieter reviews three items:

- Streaming service B: 150 monthly, card, used twice in three months. Not necessary. Review date: this week.
- Car insurance: 900 monthly, debit order, 1st. Necessary. Review date: one month before renewal, to compare quotes.
- Cloud storage: 50 monthly, card. Necessary for work files. Review date: in six months.

He cancels nothing yet. He has two clear actions with dates.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Fixed Expense Tracker and complete every column for each row: amount, frequency, due date, payment method, necessary and review date.

Sort or scan the rows where "necessary" is unticked. For each, write one next step in your own words, such as "check notice period" or "switch to cheaper plan", and add a review date.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Pick one unticked commitment and act on it this week: check its terms, downgrade it, pause it or confirm you want to keep it.

Then put your review dates into your calendar so they prompt you. One review a month is enough to keep the list current.

questions.q: You unticked "necessary" for a subscription. What is a sensible next step?
options: Check the terms, then decide whether to keep, change or cancel
questions.explain: Unticked means "review", not "cancel". Checking notice periods and fees first avoids unexpected charges.

sections.markdown:
- Every fixed expense has amount, due date, frequency, method and review date.
- You marked which commitments are necessary.
- You chose one commitment to act on this week.

lessons.title: Annualize Recurring Expenses
lessons.summary: Convert every fixed expense into a yearly and monthly figure you can compare.

sections.what: Annualizing converts weekly, monthly, quarterly and annual costs into a single yearly figure so they can be compared fairly.
sections.why: A small weekly cost and a large annual bill are hard to compare until they are on the same scale. Annual figures also show how much to set aside for irregular bills.
sections.do: Use the tracker's periods-per-year column to calculate the annual and monthly cost of each fixed expense.
sections.output: An annual and monthly total for all fixed expenses

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Fixed expenses come on different schedules, which makes them hard to compare. Annualizing puts them on one scale.

**Annual cost = amount × periods per year**

Periods per year:

- **Weekly = 52**
- **Monthly = 12**
- **Quarterly = 4**
- **Annual = 1**

The Fixed Expense Tracker does this calculation for you. Choose the frequency, enter the matching periods per year, and the annual cost appears. It also shows a **monthly equivalent** (annual cost ÷ 12), which is the amount that bill really costs you each month on average.

Why this matters:

- **Small costs add up.** 50 a week feels minor, but it is 2,600 a year.
- **Annual bills become plannable.** A 1,200 annual renewal is 100 a month if you set money aside for it. You will build that habit with the Sinking Fund Planner in Module 8.
- **Fair comparisons.** You can see which commitments take the largest share of your year and focus your reviews there.

Add up the annual cost column for your **total yearly fixed commitments**, and the monthly equivalent column for the amount your budget needs to cover each month. Compare it with your monthly income from Module 2. This shows how much of your income is already committed before any variable spending.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Pieter annualizes four items:

- Lift club: 150 weekly × 52 = 7,800 a year (650 a month).
- Phone: 600 monthly × 12 = 7,200 a year (600 a month).
- Security levy: 450 quarterly × 4 = 1,800 a year (150 a month).
- Antivirus: 900 annual × 1 = 900 a year (75 a month).

The lift club, which felt small, costs more per year than his phone. The antivirus is the one most likely to surprise him, so he plans 75 a month toward it.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Fixed Expense Tracker. For each row:

1. Confirm the frequency.
2. Enter periods per year: 52, 12, 4 or 1.
3. Check the annual cost and monthly equivalent that appear.

Look at the totals. Then mark your three largest annual costs and any quarterly or annual bills you will need to prepare for.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Take your total monthly equivalent and write it in your Financial Snapshot as your confirmed monthly fixed expenses.

List every quarterly and annual bill with its due month. When you reach Module 8, each of these becomes a sinking fund line in the Sinking Fund Planner, so the money is ready when the bill arrives.

questions.q: A cost of 200 is paid quarterly. What is its annual cost?
questions.explain: Quarterly means 4 periods per year: 200 × 4 = 800.

questions.q: How many periods per year should you use for a weekly expense?
questions.explain: There are 52 weeks in a year, so a weekly cost is multiplied by 52.

sections.markdown:
- Every fixed expense has an annual and monthly equivalent.
- You know your total yearly fixed commitments.
- You listed the irregular bills to plan for.
- **Output: Fixed Expense Tracker.**

modules.title: Variable Expenses
modules.summary: Variable spending is where most money quietly goes. This module helps you observe it honestly first, then find the patterns worth acting on.
modules.outcome: A clear view of your spending patterns: Spending Tracker + Spending Analysis

lessons.title: Separate Fixed From Variable
lessons.summary: Learn what variable spending is and set up categories that fit your life.

sections.what: Variable expenses are costs that change from week to week, such as food, transport, entertainment and personal spending.
sections.why: They are the part of your budget you can adjust most quickly, but only once you can see them clearly.
sections.do: Choose six to eight variable spending categories and record your first transactions.
sections.output: A set of spending categories and a started Variable Expense Tracker

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
In Module 3 you captured costs that repeat on a schedule. **Variable expenses** are different: the amount, and often the timing, change from week to week. Common categories:

- **Food** – groceries, takeaways, eating out, snacks at work
- **Transport** – fuel, ride-hailing, taxis, parking
- **Household purchases** – cleaning products, toiletries, small repairs
- **Personal spending** – haircuts, clothing, hobbies
- **Shopping** – online orders, electronics, homeware
- **Entertainment** – outings, events, games

**Keep categories few and clear.** Six to eight is plenty. Too many categories make tracking tedious and analysis confusing. If you are unsure where something goes, pick the closest category and add a note.

**Split food if it helps.** Groceries and eating out behave very differently. Many people find it useful to separate them.

**One purchase, one category.** If a supermarket receipt includes groceries and a small household item, you can either split it or put it under the bigger category. Choose one approach and stay consistent.

**Fixed versus variable is about behaviour, not importance.** Groceries are essential but variable. A streaming subscription is optional but fixed. The label simply tells you which tracker it belongs in.

The Variable Expense Tracker records: date, description, category, amount, whether the purchase was planned, and notes.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Zanele chooses seven categories: Groceries, Eating out, Transport, Household, Personal, Shopping, Entertainment.

Her first three entries:

- Monday, supermarket, Groceries, 650, planned.
- Monday, coffee and muffin, Eating out, 70, not planned.
- Tuesday, fuel, Transport, 500, planned.

It took two minutes. The categories already make her spending feel easier to read.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Decide your categories. Write them down and keep the list short.

Open the Variable Expense Tracker and enter every variable purchase from the past three days, using your banking app or receipts. For each, choose the category and tick Planned? if you meant to buy it before you were in the shop.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Choose a moment each day to log spending, such as when you put your phone on charge at night. Two minutes is enough.

If logging every item feels heavy, start with your card transactions from your banking app and add cash purchases from memory. Imperfect tracking is far more useful than none.

questions.q: Groceries are essential but change in amount each week. Where do they belong?
questions.explain: Fixed versus variable describes how the cost behaves, not how important it is. Groceries vary, so they are variable.

sections.markdown:
- You know the difference between fixed and variable spending.
- You chose a short list of categories.
- Your Variable Expense Tracker has its first entries.

lessons.title: Track Before You Optimize
lessons.summary: Observe your real spending for a few weeks before setting any targets.

sections.what: A tracking period where you record your variable spending as it really happens, without trying to change it yet.
sections.why: Targets set without a baseline are usually unrealistic. Knowing your real numbers lets you set limits you can actually keep.
sections.do: Track every variable expense for at least two weeks, ideally four, then total each category.
sections.output: A baseline of your real variable spending

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
When people decide to budget, the instinct is to cut immediately: "I'll spend only 500 on eating out this month." Without knowing what is normal, that number is a guess, and missing it feels like failure.

This lesson asks for something simpler: **observe first.**

For two to four weeks, log every variable expense as it actually happens. Don't try to spend less. Don't judge entries. Just record them. The aim is a **baseline**: what your spending looks like now.

Why this works:

- **You find the real numbers.** Many people discover one or two categories are much higher than they guessed, and others lower.
- **Targets become realistic.** A target based on your actual average is far easier to keep than one based on hope.
- **Less guilt, better data.** When the job is "record", there's nothing to fail at.

Tips for a useful baseline:

- **Include everything**, including cash and small amounts.
- **A full month is ideal** because it includes month-end and payday patterns.
- **Note unusual events** such as a birthday or travel so you can see them in context.
- **Use the Planned? column honestly.** It will matter in the next lesson.

At the end, total each category. That is your starting point. You'll analyse it in lesson 4.3 and use it in your Monthly Budget in Module 9.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Before tracking, Bongani guessed he spent about 2,000 a month on food.

After four weeks of tracking:

- Groceries: 2,400
- Eating out and takeaways: 1,800
- Snacks and coffee at work: 600

Total food: 4,800, more than double his guess. He doesn't feel bad about it; he now has a real number. A target of 4,000 next month is realistic. A target of 2,000 would have failed in week one.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Commit to a tracking period: two weeks minimum, four ideally. Write the start and end dates in the Notes of your first entry.

Each day, log your variable spending in the Variable Expense Tracker. At the end of week one, total each category and write the totals down. Don't change anything yet.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Keep tracking through the end of your chosen period, even on days with no spending.

If you miss a day, catch up from your banking app rather than stopping. When the period ends, total each category for the full period and record the figures. You'll analyse them in the next lesson.

questions.q: Why track spending before setting a target?
options: So targets are based on real numbers you can realistically keep
questions.explain: A baseline turns targets from guesses into realistic plans.

sections.markdown:
- You started a tracking period with clear dates.
- You are recording spending without judging it.
- You will have a real baseline for each category.

lessons.title: Find Spending Patterns
lessons.summary: Analyse your tracked spending for patterns you can plan around.

sections.what: A review of your tracked spending to find repeated purchases, high-variance categories, unplanned spending, seasonal spikes and costs you could plan in advance.
sections.why: Patterns turn a long list of transactions into a few clear decisions. They show where small changes or better planning will make the biggest difference.
sections.do: Complete the Spending Analysis and the Spending Category Review using your tracked data.
sections.output: A Spending Analysis and category-by-category review

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
With a few weeks of data, you can start looking for patterns. Five are especially useful:

1. **Repeated purchases** – the same small item bought often, such as daily coffee or frequent delivery. Each is small; together they can be large.
2. **High-variance categories** – categories that swing a lot from week to week. These are hard to budget and often benefit from a planned weekly amount.
3. **Unplanned spending** – filter for entries where Planned? is unticked. What share of your total is it? Unplanned doesn't mean wrong; it means it wasn't decided in advance.
4. **Seasonal spikes** – costs that rise at certain times: school terms, festive season, winter heating, birthdays.
5. **Expenses that could be planned in advance** – things that felt like surprises but were predictable, such as car tyres, gifts or annual events. These are strong candidates for sinking funds in Module 8.

Two tools help:

- The **Spending Analysis** is a guided reflection: totals, your top categories, your patterns and one or two decisions.
- The **Spending Category Review** looks at each category: typical month, lowest and highest amounts, the range between them, and whether to keep, plan ahead, reduce or review later.

**Focus on one to three changes**, not ten. Pick the ones that matter most to you, not the ones you think you "should" change. A budget that reflects your priorities is the one you will keep.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
After four weeks, Bongani's analysis shows:

- Repeated purchase: work coffee about 18 times, 540 in total.
- High-variance category: Eating out, from 150 to 900 a week.
- Unplanned spending: 30% of variable spending.
- Seasonal: school uniforms due in January.
- Could be planned: a birthday gift he bought in a rush.

His decisions: a set weekly amount for eating out, and sinking funds for school costs and gifts. He keeps the coffee because it matters to him.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Spending Analysis and work through every field using your tracked data. Calculate the share of unplanned spending by dividing the unplanned total by your overall total.

Then open the Spending Category Review. Add one row per category with your typical, lowest and highest amounts. Choose a decision for each row.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Put your one to three decisions into action this month. For example, set a weekly eating-out amount, or move a repeated purchase into the plan deliberately.

Use the Spending Category Review again after another month of tracking to see whether the range in each category is narrowing.

questions.q: A cost felt like a surprise but happens every year, such as school uniforms. What kind of pattern is this?
options: An expense that could be planned in advance
questions.explain: Predictable costs that arrive irregularly can be planned for, often with a sinking fund.

questions.q: What does a high-variance category mean?
options: Spending in it is always the same
Spending in it swings a lot from week to week
questions.explain: High variance means large swings, which makes the category harder to budget without a planned amount.

sections.markdown:
- You analysed your spending for five patterns.
- Each category has a typical amount, range and decision.
- You chose one to three changes to try.
- **Output: Spending Tracker + Spending Analysis.**

modules.title: Debt
modules.summary: Debt is easier to handle when it is fully visible. This module builds a complete debt inventory, explains how interest and fees affect it, and helps you compare repayment approaches for your situation.
modules.outcome: Your Debt Dashboard: Debt Tracker + Debt Plan

lessons.title: Build the Debt Inventory
lessons.summary: List every debt in one place with its key details.

sections.what: A debt inventory is a single list of everything you owe, with creditor, balance, interest rate, minimum payment, due date and remaining term.
sections.why: Debt spread across statements and apps is easy to underestimate. One clear list replaces vague worry with specific facts.
sections.do: Add every debt to the Debt Tracker using your latest statements.
sections.output: A complete debt inventory in the Debt Tracker

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A **debt inventory** brings every debt into one place. For each debt, record:

- **Creditor** – who you owe, and which account.
- **Balance** – the current amount owed, from your latest statement.
- **Interest rate** – the annual rate on the account, as a percentage.
- **Minimum payment** – the smallest required payment each period.
- **Due date** – when the payment is due.
- **Remaining term** – for loans with a fixed end date, how many months are left, where known.

Include everything:

- Credit cards and store accounts
- Personal loans
- Vehicle finance
- Home loans
- Student loans
- Buy-now-pay-later plans
- Overdrafts
- Money owed to family or friends

**Use your statements, not memory.** Balances change with interest and fees. If you can't find a rate or term, contact the lender or check your online account. Write "unknown" until you have it.

**Informal debts count.** Money owed to a relative may have no interest, but it still affects your monthly budget and your relationships. Record it.

The Debt Tracker also has an **Extra Payment** column. Leave it at zero for now; you'll use it in lesson 5.3. It also shows a total payment per debt and totals for balance, minimums and extra payments.

This can be uncomfortable. Take it one account at a time. The aim is a clear picture you can plan from.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Ruth builds her inventory:

- Credit card: balance 15,000; rate 20%; minimum 750; due 5th.
- Store account: balance 4,000; rate 22%; minimum 300; due 10th.
- Vehicle finance: balance 90,000; rate 12%; minimum 2,800; due 1st; 36 months left.
- Loan from her brother: balance 2,000; 0%; she pays 500 when she can.

Total owed: 111,000. Total minimums: 4,350 a month. Seeing it in one place is easier than she expected.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Gather the latest statement for each debt. Open the Debt Tracker and add one row per debt: name, balance, interest rate, minimum payment, due date and remaining term.

Check the totals for balance and minimums. Compare total minimums with the debt payment figure in your Financial Snapshot and update the snapshot if it differs.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
For any debt with an "unknown" rate or term, contact the lender or check your account this week and fill it in.

Add each due date to your calendar so payments aren't missed. Missed payments can add fees and further costs, so the reminders are worth setting even if you pay by debit order.

questions.q: Where should balances in your debt inventory come from?
options: Your memory of what you borrowed
Your latest statements or account records
questions.explain: Balances change with interest, fees and payments. Your latest statement shows the real figure.

sections.markdown:
- Every debt, including informal ones, is listed.
- Each has a balance, rate, minimum and due date.
- You know your total owed and total monthly minimums.

lessons.title: Understand the Cost
lessons.summary: See how interest and fees affect how quickly balances go down.

sections.what: An explanation of how interest and fees add to what you owe, and why the same payment can reduce different debts at different speeds.
sections.why: Understanding the cost of each debt helps you make informed choices, rather than treating all debts as the same.
sections.do: Estimate the monthly interest on each debt and note any fees from your account terms.
sections.output: A view of what each debt costs you each month

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
When you make a payment on a debt, part of it typically covers **interest** and **fees**, and the rest reduces the **balance**. The higher the interest and fees, the less of your payment goes toward the balance.

**A rough monthly interest estimate:**

**Balance × annual interest rate ÷ 12**

For example, 10,000 at 18% a year: 10,000 × 0.18 ÷ 12 = about 150 in interest that month. If the minimum payment is 400, roughly 250 reduces the balance.

This is an approximation. Lenders calculate interest in different ways (daily, monthly, on average balances), and many accounts also charge **fees**, such as monthly service fees, admin fees or late-payment fees. **Use your actual account terms where available.** Your statement or agreement shows the rate, fees and how interest is charged.

What this tells you:

- **Minimum payments can mean slow progress** on high-interest accounts, because much of the payment covers interest.
- **Fees add up.** A monthly service fee is a fixed cost of having that debt.
- **Rates can change.** Some debts have variable rates linked to wider interest rates. Check your agreement.

Lending rules, interest caps and consumer protections differ between countries. If you have questions about your rights or your terms, check with your lender, your country's official consumer or credit regulator, or a qualified debt counsellor or adviser.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Ruth estimates monthly interest:

- Credit card: 15,000 × 0.20 ÷ 12 = about 250. Of her 750 minimum, roughly 500 reduces the balance. Her statement also shows a 60 service fee.
- Store account: 4,000 × 0.22 ÷ 12 = about 73. Of 300, roughly 227 goes to the balance.
- Vehicle finance: 90,000 × 0.12 ÷ 12 = about 900. Of 2,800, roughly 1,900 reduces the balance.

She now sees each debt's cost in the same terms.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
For each debt in your Debt Tracker, use the rough formula to estimate this month's interest. Write the estimate and any fees from your statement in the Notes of your own records, or alongside the tracker.

Then compare each estimate with your statement, if it shows interest charged. Note any big difference; it may mean the lender calculates interest differently.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Read the terms or latest statement for your largest debt. Find three things: the interest rate, how it is charged, and any monthly or late-payment fees.

If anything is unclear, write down your question and ask the lender directly. Knowing the real terms is the foundation for the repayment plan in the next lesson.

questions.q: Using the rough formula, what is the approximate monthly interest on 12,000 at 15% a year?
questions.explain: 12,000 × 0.15 ÷ 12 = 150. Real interest depends on how your lender calculates it, so check your terms.

questions.q: Why might a minimum payment reduce a high-interest balance slowly?
options: A large part of the payment may go to interest and fees
questions.explain: When interest and fees take a large share of the payment, less goes toward the balance.

sections.markdown:
- You understand how interest and fees affect progress.
- You estimated the monthly interest on each debt.
- You know where to find your real account terms.

lessons.title: Create a Repayment Plan
lessons.summary: Compare repayment approaches and choose one that fits your circumstances.

sections.what: A repayment plan sets how much you pay toward each debt, including any extra payment, and in what order.
sections.why: A plan turns debt from a background worry into a schedule you can follow and review.
sections.do: Use the Debt Payoff Planner to compare approaches, then record your chosen extra payments in the Debt Tracker.
sections.output: A Debt Plan with chosen approach, extra payments and review date

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A repayment plan answers three questions:

1. **Can I keep up with every minimum payment?** This comes first. If not, see the note at the end.
2. **How much extra, if any, can I pay?** Use your Financial Snapshot and Monthly Budget to find a realistic amount.
3. **Where does the extra go first?**

People commonly compare approaches like these:

- **Smallest balance first** – pay minimums on all debts and put extra toward the smallest balance. Some people find quick wins motivating.
- **Highest interest rate first** – put extra toward the debt with the highest rate. This typically reduces total interest paid, depending on terms and fees.
- **Hybrid or other priorities** – for example, clearing a debt with high fees, a debt owed to family, or one causing the most stress.

**No single approach is right for everyone.** The best choice depends on your balances, rates, fees, income stability, other goals and what keeps you going. Some people also consider whether to build an emergency reserve alongside debt repayment, which you'll think about in Modules 6 and 7.

For each debt, the worksheet captures: current balance, minimum payment, interest rate, extra payment capacity, and a target date if you choose one.

**If minimums aren't manageable,** contact your lenders early to ask about options, and consider speaking to a qualified, registered debt counsellor or a free advice service in your country. Options such as consolidation or formal arrangements have rules and costs that vary by country, so get qualified guidance before deciding.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Ruth has 1,000 a month extra. She compares:

- Smallest balance first: her brother's 2,000 loan, then the store account.
- Highest rate first: the store account (22%), then the credit card (20%).

Both approaches put the store account early. She chooses to clear her brother's loan first because it matters to her, then switch to highest rate. She sets a review date in three months. It's her decision, based on her priorities.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Debt Payoff Planner. Work through each field: list your debts in each order, rate how each approach fits your priorities, and note your extra payment capacity.

Choose an approach, or "not decided yet" if you need more information. Then add your extra payment amounts to the Debt Tracker and check the new total payments.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Make this month's payments according to your plan, and record any extra payments in the Debt Tracker.

Update each balance from your statements once a month. On your review date, ask: is this approach still working for me? Changing approach after a review is fine. You'll include your planned debt payments in your Monthly Budget in Module 9.

questions.q: Which statement about debt repayment approaches is accurate?
options: Smallest balance first is always best
Highest interest first is always best
The right approach depends on your circumstances and priorities
Only minimum payments should ever be made
questions.explain: Different approaches suit different situations. Compare them using your real balances, rates, fees and priorities.

questions.q: What should come first in any repayment plan?
options: Choosing which debt to pay extra on
Making sure every minimum payment can be covered
Setting a target date for every debt
questions.explain: Missing minimums can add fees and further costs. Covering them comes before extra payments.

sections.markdown:
- You compared repayment approaches without assuming one is best.
- You chose an approach, extra payments and a review date.
- Your Debt Tracker shows your full plan.
- **Output: Debt Tracker + Debt Plan.**

modules.title: Savings
modules.summary: Savings work best when every amount has a clear purpose and a target. This module turns general savings into a tracked system of specific goals.

lessons.title: Give Savings a Job
lessons.summary: Assign a clear purpose to every amount you save.

sections.what: Giving savings a job means deciding what each amount is for: an emergency reserve, a short-term purchase, an annual expense, a long-term goal or a planned large purchase.
sections.why: Money with a purpose is easier to protect and easier to build. Savings without a job tend to get spent on whatever comes up next.
sections.do: List your savings purposes and give each one a name in the Savings Tracker.
sections.output: A list of named savings goals, each with a purpose

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
"Saving" is often one vague pot. When an unexpected cost or a tempting purchase comes up, the pot gets used, and it is hard to tell whether that was a good use or not.

**Giving savings a job** fixes this. Each amount has a purpose:

- **Emergency reserve** – for unexpected, urgent costs such as a sudden repair or a gap in income. You'll plan this in detail in Module 7.
- **Short-term purchase** – something within a few months, like a new phone or a course fee.
- **Annual expense** – a known yearly bill such as a vehicle licence or insurance excess, covered by sinking funds in Module 8.
- **Long-term goal** – further out, such as education or a home deposit.
- **Planned large purchase** – a car, furniture, a major trip.

**Name each goal specifically.** "Car service, March" is more motivating and easier to protect than "savings".

**Separate where it helps.** Some banks let you create sub-accounts or "pockets". Others use separate accounts. If yours doesn't, the Savings Tracker can still show how one balance is split between jobs.

**Long-term goals and investing:** for long-term goals, people often consider products other than a savings account. Those choices depend on your circumstances, timeframe and country-specific rules, so this course does not recommend any product. For decisions about investing or retirement products, speak to a qualified, registered financial adviser.

Start with three to five jobs. You can always add more later.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Musa has 12,000 in one savings account and no plan for it. He gives it jobs:

- Emergency reserve: 7,000
- Car service, March (annual expense): 2,000
- New laptop (short-term purchase): 3,000

The total is the same 12,000. But when a friend suggests a weekend away, Musa can see none of it is spare. If he wants the trip, it needs its own job.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Write down every reason you want to save, then group them under the five purposes.

Open the Savings Tracker. Add one row per goal with a specific name and its purpose. If you already have savings, split the current amount across your goals in the Current column so it adds up to your real balance.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
If your bank allows sub-accounts or named pockets, consider creating one per goal, or at least separating your emergency reserve from everything else. Check any fees or withdrawal rules first.

If not, update your Savings Tracker whenever you add or withdraw money, noting which goal it belongs to.

questions.q: Why give each amount of savings a specific job?
options: It makes savings earn more interest
It makes the money easier to protect and track toward a purpose
It replaces the need for a budget
questions.explain: A clear purpose helps you decide whether a withdrawal fits the plan and shows progress on each goal.

sections.markdown:
- Each of your savings goals has a purpose.
- Every goal has a specific name.
- Your current savings are split across goals.

lessons.title: Set Specific Targets
lessons.summary: Give every savings goal a target amount, date and contribution.

sections.what: Setting a target means defining each goal's target amount, current amount, remaining amount, target date and contribution frequency.
sections.why: A specific target turns a hope into a plan. You can see exactly how much to put aside, how often, and whether you are on track.
sections.do: Complete the target, current, contribution and target date columns for each goal in the Savings Tracker.
sections.output: A Savings Tracker with targets and contributions for every goal

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
For each savings goal, define:

- **Goal** – the specific name.
- **Target amount** – how much you need.
- **Current amount** – how much is already set aside.
- **Remaining amount** – target minus current. The tracker calculates this for you.
- **Target date** – when you need the money.
- **Contribution and frequency** – how much you'll add, and how often (weekly, every payday, monthly).

**Working out a contribution:**

**Remaining amount ÷ number of contributions before the target date = contribution per period**

For example, 6,000 remaining over 12 months is 500 a month. Over 24 fortnightly paydays it is 250 each payday. This is arithmetic, not a recommendation; the right amount depends on what fits your budget.

**When the numbers don't fit:** add up the contributions across all your goals. If the total is more than you can afford, you have three levers:

1. **Move the target date** later.
2. **Lower the target** amount.
3. **Prioritise** – fund the most important goals first and pause others.

All three are valid choices. A realistic plan you keep is better than an ambitious one you abandon.

**Setting a target amount:** use real quotes or prices where possible. For your emergency reserve, Module 7 walks you through choosing a target that suits your circumstances, because there is no single right number for everyone.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Musa's laptop goal: target 12,000, current 3,000, remaining 9,000, target date in 9 months. 9,000 ÷ 9 = 1,000 a month.

That's more than he can manage alongside his other goals. He moves the target date to 12 months: 9,000 ÷ 12 = 750 a month. It fits, and he keeps the goal.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Savings Tracker. For each goal, fill in the target amount, target date, contribution and frequency. Check the Remaining column.

Calculate each contribution using remaining ÷ number of contributions. Then add up your monthly contributions across all goals. If the total doesn't fit, adjust one goal's date, target or priority and note why.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Choose the day you'll make each contribution. Many people find it easiest on payday, before variable spending starts.

Write your total planned savings contribution in your Financial Snapshot. You'll include it as its own line in your Monthly Budget in Module 9, so saving becomes part of the plan rather than whatever is left over.

questions.q: A goal has a target of 8,000 and a current amount of 2,000. What is the remaining amount?
questions.explain: Remaining = target − current = 8,000 − 2,000 = 6,000.

questions.q: Your planned contributions are more than you can afford. Which is a reasonable response?
options: Move a target date, lower a target or prioritise goals
questions.explain: Adjusting dates, targets or priorities keeps the plan realistic so you can stick with it.

sections.markdown:
- Every goal has a target, date and contribution.
- The tracker shows how much remains on each goal.
- Your total contributions fit your budget.

lessons.title: Automate Where Appropriate
lessons.summary: Use recurring transfers, where available, so saving happens without relying on memory.

sections.what: Automation means setting up recurring transfers, if your bank or provider supports them, so savings contributions happen on schedule.
sections.why: Saving relies less on willpower and memory when it happens automatically. It also stops contributions from being skipped in busy months.
sections.do: Check what your bank offers and set up, or plan, one recurring transfer for a savings goal.
sections.output: At least one savings contribution scheduled automatically, or a clear manual routine

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
If your bank or provider supports it, a **recurring transfer** can move money to savings on a set day without you having to remember. This reduces the chance of a contribution being skipped because you were busy or because the money was spent first.

**How people commonly set it up:**

- **Time it just after payday.** Saving first means the contribution isn't competing with spending.
- **Match your Savings Tracker.** Use the same amount and frequency you set in lesson 6.2.
- **One transfer per goal, or one combined transfer.** Some people send one amount to savings and split it between goals in the tracker.
- **Name the transfer** after its goal so your statement is easy to read.

**Where appropriate is the key phrase.** Automation isn't right in every situation:

- If your **income is variable**, a fixed automatic amount could leave you short in a lean month. Some people automate a small base amount and add more manually in good months.
- **Check fees and limits.** Some accounts charge for transfers or limit withdrawals.
- **Make sure fixed bills are covered first**, so a transfer doesn't cause a failed debit order or overdraft fee.

**If automation isn't available**, create a manual routine: a calendar reminder on payday, and a quick update to the Savings Tracker when the transfer is made.

**Review regularly.** Each month, update Current amounts in the tracker and check you're on track for each target date.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Musa's salary arrives on the 25th. He sets up two recurring transfers on the 26th:

- 750 to a pocket named "Laptop".
- 500 to a pocket named "Emergency reserve".

His annual car service is saved manually, because the amount varies with his mileage. He sets a reminder on the 26th to make that transfer and update the tracker.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Log in to your banking app or contact your bank and find out:

1. Can you set up recurring transfers?
2. Can you create named sub-accounts or pockets?
3. Are there fees or withdrawal limits?

Then, in the Savings Tracker, tick Automated? for any goal you've scheduled, and note the transfer day.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Set up one recurring transfer this week for your highest-priority goal, if your bank supports it and your income allows it. If not, set a payday reminder instead.

At month-end, update each Current amount. Your emergency reserve will get its own detailed tracker in Module 7, the Emergency Fund Tracker, where you'll set a target that fits your circumstances.

questions.q: When might a fixed automatic savings transfer need extra care?
options: When income is variable and some months are lean
questions.explain: With variable income, a fixed amount could leave you short. Some people automate a small base and add more in good months.

sections.markdown:
- You checked what your bank offers.
- At least one contribution is automated or on a clear manual routine.
- Your Savings Tracker shows which goals are automated.
- **Output: Savings Tracker.**

modules.title: Emergency Fund
modules.summary: Set aside money for the unexpected so a surprise cost does not undo the rest of your plan. You choose a target that fits your circumstances and build towards it step by step.
modules.outcome: Your Emergency Fund Plan and Emergency Fund Tracker

lessons.title: What an Emergency Fund Is
lessons.summary: Understand what an emergency reserve is for, and what it is not for.

sections.what: An emergency fund is money set aside for unexpected or urgent expenses, kept separate from everyday spending.
sections.why: Without a reserve, a surprise cost often lands on a credit card or loan, or pushes other bills late. A reserve gives you time to respond calmly.
sections.do: Write your own definition of an emergency and list three things that would and would not count.
sections.output: A personal definition of what your emergency fund is for

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
An **emergency fund** is money you deliberately keep aside for costs that are **unexpected, necessary and urgent**. It is not a holiday fund, a shopping fund or an annual-bill fund. Those are planned costs, and they get their own place in Module 8.

A useful test has three questions:

1. **Is it unexpected?** You did not know it was coming, or not when.
2. **Is it necessary?** Leaving it would cause real harm to your health, home, income or safety.
3. **Is it urgent?** It needs paying soon, not next year.

If the answer to all three is yes, it is probably an emergency. Common examples include an urgent medical or dental cost, an essential car or appliance repair, a sudden drop in income, or an urgent trip to support family.

Things that usually are **not** emergencies: a sale, a birthday, the annual insurance premium, school fees, or a phone upgrade. These are predictable, even if they feel sudden when they arrive.

**Where the money lives matters.** Many people keep their reserve in a separate account from their everyday spending, so it is easy to reach in a real emergency but not so easy that it drifts into daily use. What is available, and on what terms, depends on your bank or provider and your country, so check the details directly with them.

An emergency fund does not stop bad things happening. It changes how much damage they do to the rest of your plan. That is the job.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Thandi's fridge stops working. It is unexpected, she needs it to store food safely, and it cannot wait two months. That passes all three questions, so she uses her emergency fund.

A month later her car licence renewal arrives. It feels sudden, but it happens every year on the same date. It fails the "unexpected" question, so she pays it from her sinking fund instead and adds it to her annual calendar so it never surprises her again.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Take five minutes and write:

1. Your one-sentence definition of an emergency, in your own words.
2. Three things that **would** count for you.
3. Three things that **would not** count, even if they feel urgent at the time.
4. Where your reserve is kept now (or where you plan to keep it).

Put your definition in the review note of the first row of your Emergency Fund Tracker so you see it every time you update it.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: This week, if you are tempted to use money set aside for emergencies, run the three questions first: unexpected, necessary, urgent. If one answer is no, look for another source, usually a sinking fund or next month's budget. Notice which "almost emergencies" come up. Each one is a clue to a planned cost you can add to Module 8.

questions.q: Which of these is most likely an emergency under the three-question test?
options: Urgent repair to a broken geyser or water heater
A large discount on a television
questions.explain: The repair is unexpected, necessary and urgent. The others are predictable or optional, so they belong in sinking funds or the monthly budget.

questions.q: Why do many people keep the emergency fund separate from everyday spending money?
options: It is required by law in every country
It keeps the money reachable but less likely to be spent by accident
It removes the need to review it
questions.explain: Separation is about clarity and protection from everyday drift. Returns and rules depend on your provider and country.

sections.markdown:
- You know what an emergency fund is for, and what it is not for.
- You have a personal definition of an emergency.
- You can use the three-question test before dipping into your reserve.

lessons.title: Define Your Target
lessons.summary: Choose an emergency-fund target that fits your circumstances, not someone else's rule.

sections.what: Your target is the amount you are aiming to hold in your emergency reserve, based on your essential costs and situation.
sections.why: There is no single correct number for everyone. A target that fits your life is one you can actually reach and use.
sections.do: Work out your essential monthly costs, consider your circumstances, and choose a first milestone and a fuller target.
sections.output: A personal emergency-fund target with a first milestone

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
You will hear many rules of thumb about emergency funds. They can be a starting point for thinking, but **no single number is right for everyone**. The right target for you depends on your circumstances.

Start with your **essential monthly costs**: housing, utilities, basic food, transport to earn income, insurance premiums, minimum debt payments, and anything you must pay to keep your household running. Your Financial Snapshot and Fixed Expense Tracker already hold most of this.

Then consider the factors that can push your target up or down:

- **Income stability.** Steady salary, commission, freelance or seasonal income?
- **Dependants.** Are others relying on your income?
- **Insurance and benefits.** What would cover part of a shock, and what would not?
- **Other support.** Is there a partner's income or other support you could realistically rely on?
- **Known risks.** An older car, a health need, a contract ending.

A practical way to structure it:

1. **First milestone:** a smaller amount that covers a common surprise, such as one repair or one urgent bill. Reaching this quickly matters.
2. **Fuller target:** a number of months of essential costs that you choose after thinking through the factors above.

If you have high-cost debt, you may be balancing building a reserve against paying that down. That trade-off depends on your situation. If you are unsure, a qualified, independent adviser or a reputable non-profit money service in your country can help.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Sam's essential costs are about 10,000 a month in his currency. His income is commission-based and varies, and he supports one child.

He sets a **first milestone of 5,000**, enough for one big repair. After thinking about his variable income, he chooses a **fuller target of 40,000**, roughly four months of essentials. His sister, on a steady salary with no dependants, chose a smaller fuller target. Both choices are reasonable for their situations.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
1. Add up your essential monthly costs from your Financial Snapshot and Fixed Expense Tracker.
2. Rate each factor (income stability, dependants, insurance, other support, known risks) as "lowers my need" or "raises my need".
3. Choose a first milestone you could reach in a few months.
4. Choose a fuller target, written as an amount and as months of essential costs.
5. Enter the fuller target in the Target column of your Emergency Fund Tracker.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Write your two numbers somewhere you will see them: first milestone and fuller target. Plan to revisit the fuller target when your circumstances change, such as a new job, a new dependant, or a change in insurance cover. A target is a decision you can update, not a test you pass or fail.

questions.q: What is the best starting point for an emergency-fund target?
options: Your own essential monthly costs and circumstances
The highest amount you can imagine
questions.explain: Your essential costs and circumstances shape a target that fits you. No single number is universally correct.

questions.q: Why set a first milestone before a fuller target?
options: It replaces the need for a fuller target
It gives quick protection against common surprises and builds momentum
It avoids having to track progress
questions.explain: A smaller first milestone protects you sooner and makes the larger target feel reachable.

sections.markdown:
- You know your essential monthly costs.
- You have considered your income stability, dependants, insurance and support.
- You have a first milestone and a fuller target.

lessons.title: Build Gradually
lessons.summary: Turn your target into a steady contribution plan you can track and review.

sections.what: Building gradually means saving a regular, realistic amount towards your target and tracking the balance over time.
sections.why: Large targets feel impossible in one go. Small, regular contributions with a clear tracker make progress visible.
sections.do: Set your current amount, target, monthly contribution and review date, then fill in your first row.
sections.output: A live Emergency Fund Tracker

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A target only helps if there is a plan to reach it. Your plan has four parts:

- **Current amount:** what is set aside today, even if it is zero.
- **Target:** the milestone or fuller target from the last lesson.
- **Contribution:** how much you add each month (or each pay cycle).
- **Review date:** when you will check progress and adjust.

To find a contribution, look at what your monthly budget can realistically carry. It is better to commit to a smaller amount you keep up than a larger amount you abandon. You can also add **windfalls**, such as a bonus, refund or gift, if you choose to.

A rough timeline: **remaining amount ÷ monthly contribution = months to reach target.** This is a guide, not a promise. Income changes and real emergencies will move it.

If your bank or provider supports scheduled transfers, setting one up for payday can reduce the need to remember. Check fees and terms with your provider.

**When you use the fund,** that is the fund working, not failing. Record the withdrawal, write a short note on what happened, and plan how to rebuild. Some people pause other savings briefly to refill the reserve; others rebuild slowly alongside them. Choose what fits your budget.

**Review the plan** at least every few months, and whenever your essential costs or circumstances change.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Lerato has 2,000 saved. Her first milestone is 6,000. Her budget can carry 500 a month.

Remaining: 6,000 − 2,000 = 4,000. At 500 a month that is about 8 months. In month 3 she uses 1,500 for a car repair. She records it in her tracker with a note, keeps contributing 500, and moves her review date one month later. No panic, just an update.
