sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your Emergency Fund Tracker and fill in your first row:

1. Choose the month.
2. Enter this month's contribution (zero is fine if you are just starting).
3. Enter your current balance after that contribution.
4. Enter your target. The Remaining column calculates target minus balance.
5. Add a review note, such as your definition of an emergency or the date of your next review.

Then work out your rough timeline: remaining ÷ contribution.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: This month, make one contribution, however small, and record it. Put your review date in your calendar. Each month, add a new row so the Remaining column shows your progress. If you withdraw money for a real emergency, record the lower balance and write what happened in the review note. Your tracker should tell the honest story.

questions.q: Your target is 9,000, your balance is 3,000, and you contribute 500 a month. Roughly how long until you reach the target?
questions.explain: Remaining is 9,000 − 3,000 = 6,000. 6,000 ÷ 500 = 12 months, as a rough guide.

questions.q: You use part of your emergency fund for a genuine urgent repair. What is the most helpful next step?
options: Stop tracking because the plan failed
Record the withdrawal, note what happened, and plan how to rebuild
questions.explain: Using the fund for a real emergency is its purpose. Recording and rebuilding keeps the system honest and current.

sections.markdown:
- You have a current amount, target, contribution and review date.
- Your Emergency Fund Tracker has its first row.
- You know how to handle a withdrawal without abandoning the plan.

modules.title: Goals & Sinking Funds
modules.summary: Plan for irregular and known future expenses before they turn into emergencies. You set clear goals and break each one into a regular contribution.
modules.outcome: Your Financial Goals Planner and Sinking Fund Planner

lessons.title: What Is a Sinking Fund?
lessons.summary: Learn how setting money aside for known future costs removes many 'surprise' expenses.

sections.what: A sinking fund is money deliberately set aside, bit by bit, for a known future expense.
sections.why: Many costs that feel like emergencies are actually predictable. Sinking funds spread them out so they do not land all at once.
sections.do: List the irregular expenses you know are coming in 2026 and choose which ones need a sinking fund.
sections.output: A list of your financial goals and irregular expenses

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A **sinking fund** is money you set aside regularly for an expense you **know is coming**, even if it does not happen every month. Instead of finding a large amount at once, you save a smaller amount each month until it is ready.

Common examples:

- Annual insurance premiums or licence renewals
- Gifts and festive season costs
- Holidays and travel
- Car maintenance and tyres
- School fees, uniforms and stationery
- Electronics that will need replacing
- Large planned purchases, such as furniture

**Sinking fund or emergency fund?** An emergency fund covers the unexpected. A sinking fund covers the expected. If you can name the cost and roughly when it arrives, it usually belongs in a sinking fund. Keeping them separate protects your emergency reserve for real emergencies.

**Goals are bigger than sinking funds.** A financial goal is anything you are working towards: a deposit, paying off a debt, a course, a trip. Some goals are funded through sinking funds. Others, like a debt goal, are handled in your debt plan. Writing all of them down in one place helps you see what you are asking your money to do in 2026, and whether it is realistic.

You do not need a separate bank account for every fund. Some people use one savings account and track each fund on paper or in a spreadsheet. Others use separate "pockets" if their bank offers them. Choose what is simple for you.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Every December, Ayanda felt broke. Looking back at the year, she found the same costs each time: gifts (3,000), a family trip (6,000) and school items in January (2,400).

None of these were surprises. They were simply unplanned. She now lists them as goals, and three of them become sinking funds with monthly contributions. December still costs money, but the money is already there.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Financial Goals Planner and add rows for:

1. Every irregular expense you expect in 2026 (look at last year's bank statements for clues).
2. Any bigger goals you are working towards, including savings and debt goals.

For each one, add a rough target amount, a target date and a priority. In the "Sinking fund?" column, mark the ones you will save for gradually.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: This week, when a non-monthly cost comes up, such as a renewal notice, a school letter or a friend's wedding invite, add it to your Financial Goals Planner straight away. Over a few weeks your list becomes a reliable map of the costs that used to catch you off guard.

questions.q: Which expense is the best fit for a sinking fund?
options: Annual car insurance renewal in March
questions.explain: The insurance renewal is known in advance, so you can save for it gradually. The others are unexpected and belong to the emergency fund.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of a sinking fund?
options: It spreads a known cost over several months so it does not land all at once
It removes the need for a budget
questions.explain: Sinking funds turn one large predictable cost into smaller regular contributions.

sections.markdown:
- You know the difference between a sinking fund and an emergency fund.
- You have listed your known irregular expenses and bigger goals.
- You have marked which goals will use a sinking fund.

lessons.title: The Basic Formula
lessons.summary: Use one simple calculation to turn any known expense into a monthly amount.

sections.what: The sinking fund formula divides the amount you still need by the number of contributions left.
sections.why: It turns a vague goal into a concrete monthly number you can put into your budget.
sections.do: Calculate the monthly contribution for at least three of your goals.
sections.output: A suggested contribution for each sinking fund

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
The basic formula is:

> **Goal amount ÷ number of contribution periods = target contribution**

**Example:** a 600 annual expense ÷ 12 months = 50 a month. This example is illustrative, not financial advice.

If you already have some money set aside, use the amount still needed:

> **(Target − current amount) ÷ periods left = suggested contribution**

A few practical points:

- **Count periods carefully.** If the cost is due in June and you start in January, you have about 5 or 6 monthly contributions, depending on when it is paid. Fewer periods means a higher amount.
- **Match your pay cycle.** If you are paid weekly or every two weeks, you can count periods that way instead of months.
- **Round up slightly** if prices may rise or the amount is an estimate. Check real quotes when you can.
- **Add it all up.** The total of all your sinking fund contributions has to fit in your monthly budget. If it does not, you have choices: move a target date, reduce a target, change the priority, or find room elsewhere.

When the total is too high, that is useful information, not failure. It shows you, early, that your plans need more money than you have, and gives you time to decide what matters most.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Nomsa has three goals:

- Car service: 3,000 in 6 months, 0 saved. 3,000 ÷ 6 = 500 a month.
- Holiday: 9,000 in 12 months, 3,000 saved. (9,000 − 3,000) ÷ 12 = 500 a month.
- New laptop: 6,000 in 10 months, 1,000 saved. (6,000 − 1,000) ÷ 10 = 500 a month.

Total: 1,500 a month. Her budget can carry 1,000, so she moves the laptop out by 10 months, which brings it down to 250 a month and her total to 1,250. Still too high, she trims the holiday target. A choice made calmly in January, not in a rush in December.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
For three goals from your Financial Goals Planner:

1. Write the target amount and how much you already have.
2. Count the contribution periods left before the due date.
3. Calculate (target − current) ÷ periods left.
4. Add the three results together.

Does the total fit your budget? If not, note which goal you would move first.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Choose the one sinking fund that would cause the most stress if it were not ready, and start contributing to it this month. Even a partial contribution reduces the pressure later. Next month, add the next fund. Building them one by one is easier than starting all at once.

questions.q: You need 1,200 for a renewal in 6 months and have 0 saved. What is the suggested monthly contribution?
The total of your sinking fund contributions is higher than your budget can carry. What is a sensible response?
options: Adjust target dates, amounts or priorities until it fits
Use the emergency fund each month
questions.explain: The formula shows the trade-off early so you can choose what to move or reduce.

sections.markdown:
- You can calculate a sinking fund contribution with the basic formula.
- You have calculated contributions for at least three goals.
- You know how to adjust when the total does not fit.

lessons.title: Build Your Sinking Fund Planner
lessons.summary: Set up a planner that calculates what remains and what to contribute for every fund.

sections.what: The Sinking Fund Planner tracks each fund's target, current balance, remaining amount and suggested contribution.
sections.why: With every fund in one table, you can see the full monthly commitment and update it as balances grow.
sections.do: Enter each sinking fund in the planner and let the formulas calculate remaining and suggested contributions.
sections.output: A working Sinking Fund Planner

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Your planner tracks six things for each fund:

- **Goal:** what the money is for.
- **Target:** the amount you need.
- **Current:** how much is already set aside.
- **Remaining:** target − current. Calculated for you.
- **Periods left:** how many contributions remain before the due date.
- **Suggested contribution:** (target − current) ÷ periods left. Calculated for you.

The planner also has a **target date** column, so you can see what is coming next.

**Each month, update two numbers per fund:** the current balance and the periods left. The suggested contribution then recalculates. If you fell behind one month, the number goes up a little. If you added extra, it goes down. Either way, you always see the honest amount needed from here.

**When a fund is used,** record the expense, reset the current amount (often to zero), and, if the cost repeats, set a new target date and periods left for next year.

**Keep the list focused.** Too many tiny funds can become hard to manage. If several small costs are similar, such as gifts for different people, you can combine them into one fund.

The total of the Suggested Contribution column is the amount your monthly budget needs to set aside for sinking funds. You will carry this into Module 9.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Pieter's planner shows:

- Car service: target 3,000, current 1,000, remaining 2,000, periods left 4, suggested 500.
- Gifts: target 2,400, current 600, remaining 1,800, periods left 6, suggested 300.
- School items: target 1,800, current 1,200, remaining 600, periods left 2, suggested 300.

The total suggested contribution is 1,100. That becomes the "Sinking funds" line in his monthly budget.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown: Open the Sinking Fund Planner and add a row for each fund from your Financial Goals Planner that you marked as a sinking fund. Enter goal, target, current, periods left and target date. Check that Remaining and Suggested Contribution make sense. Then read the total at the bottom of the Suggested Contribution column and write it down for your monthly budget.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Pick a fixed day each month, such as the day after payday, to make your sinking fund contributions and update the planner. Update the current balance and reduce periods left by one. If your bank allows scheduled transfers, you may choose to set one up for the total. Check fees and terms with your provider first.

questions.q: In the planner, how is Remaining calculated?
questions.explain: Remaining is the target minus what you already have.

questions.q: You missed a contribution last month. What happens to the suggested contribution after you update the planner?
options: It goes up slightly, because the same remaining amount is spread over fewer periods
questions.explain: Fewer periods with the same remaining amount means a slightly higher contribution, which shows the honest amount needed from here.

sections.markdown:
- Every sinking fund is in your planner.
- Remaining and suggested contributions are calculated for you.
- You know your total monthly sinking fund amount for your budget.

modules.title: Build Your Monthly Budget
modules.summary: Bring income, expenses, debt, savings and sinking funds together into one monthly plan. You see the complete picture before you spend.

lessons.title: Start With Income
lessons.summary: Begin your budget with the money you realistically expect to receive this month.

sections.what: Your budget starts with expected income: every amount you realistically expect to receive in the month.
sections.why: Every other number in your budget depends on this one. Overestimating income is one of the most common reasons budgets break.
sections.do: Enter each expected income source for the month as Income rows in your Monthly Budget.
sections.output: The income section of your Monthly Budget

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A budget is a plan for money you **expect** to have. So it starts with income.

Use your Income Tracker and Income Calendar from Module 2. For the month you are planning, list each source separately:

- Salary or wages (the amount that actually reaches your account after deductions)
- Freelance or business income
- Commission or bonuses
- Side income
- Benefits or other legitimate income

**Use the amount you actually receive.** For most employed people that is take-home pay after tax and other deductions. How tax and deductions work depends on your country and situation, so check your payslip or an official source if you are unsure.

**For variable income, plan conservatively.** Do not assume your best month will repeat. Some people plan with a lower, typical month and treat anything above it as a bonus to allocate once it arrives. Others use the average of their last few lower months. Either way, base the budget on money you are reasonably confident will arrive.

**Timing matters too.** If income arrives on different dates, note them. A bill due on the 1st cannot be paid from income that arrives on the 25th unless you plan for it.

Only include money that is genuinely yours to spend this month. Loans, credit limits and money you are holding for someone else are not income.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Kagiso has a salary of 15,000 take-home and freelance work that has ranged from 1,000 to 5,000 a month this year.

He enters two Income rows: Salary, planned 15,000, and Freelance, planned 1,000, the lower end of his range. When a 4,000 freelance month comes in, he records the actual amount and decides where the extra 3,000 goes, rather than spending it before it arrives.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your Monthly Budget and add a row for each income source this month:

1. Category: the source name.
2. Type: Income.
3. Planned: the amount you realistically expect.
4. Notes: the expected date, and "variable" if the amount changes.

Leave Actual blank for now. You will fill it in when the money arrives.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: This month, when each payment arrives, enter the actual amount in your budget straight away. If something arrives late or is lower than planned, note it. After a couple of months, you will know how reliable each income source is, which makes your next budget more accurate.

questions.q: Your freelance income has ranged from 2,000 to 8,000 a month. What is a conservative planning approach?
options: Plan with a lower, typical amount and allocate extra when it arrives
Leave it out and never record it
questions.explain: Planning with a lower amount reduces the risk of committing money that does not arrive.

questions.q: Which of these counts as income in your budget?
options: Take-home pay that reaches your account
Money you are holding for a friend
A loan offer you have not accepted
questions.explain: Only money that is genuinely yours to spend this month counts as income.

sections.markdown:
- Every expected income source for the month is in your budget.
- Variable income is planned conservatively.
- You know when each amount is expected to arrive.

lessons.title: Allocate the Money
lessons.summary: Give each part of your income a job before the month begins.

sections.what: Allocating means deciding in advance how your income will be split across fixed costs, variable spending, debt, savings and sinking funds.
sections.why: When money has a job before you spend, everyday choices get easier and fewer things are forgotten.
sections.do: Add planned amounts for every Fixed, Variable, Debt, Savings and Sinking fund row in your Monthly Budget.
sections.output: A fully allocated Monthly Budget

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Once you know your income, you decide where it goes. Your Monthly Budget uses five types of outgoing rows:

1. **Fixed:** costs that stay mostly the same, such as rent, insurance, phone, internet and subscriptions. Copy these from your Fixed Expense Tracker.
2. **Variable:** costs that change, such as groceries, transport, entertainment and personal spending. Use the baseline you observed in Module 4, not an ideal you have never reached.
3. **Debt:** at least the minimum payment for each debt, plus any extra payment you chose in your debt plan.
4. **Savings:** your emergency fund contribution and other savings from Modules 6 and 7.
5. **Sinking fund:** the total suggested contribution from your Sinking Fund Planner, or one row per fund.

**A sensible order** for many people: essentials first (housing, utilities, food, transport to work), then minimum debt payments, then savings and sinking funds, then flexible spending. Your priorities may differ, and that is fine.

**Be realistic.** A grocery amount that is far below what you actually spend will not last a week. It is better to start with an honest number and reduce it gradually, if you choose to.

**Leave a small buffer.** A "miscellaneous" or "buffer" line catches small forgotten costs without breaking the plan.

If your planned outgoings are higher than your income, you have a gap to close before the month starts. The next lesson shows how to see it clearly.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Zanele's income is 20,000. She allocates:

- Fixed: rent 7,000, insurance 1,000, phone and data 500.
- Variable: groceries 3,500, transport 1,500, personal 1,000.
- Debt: store card 800, car loan 2,000.
- Savings: emergency fund 1,000.
- Sinking fund: 1,200.
- Buffer: 300.

Total allocated: 19,800. She has a clear picture before spending anything.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
In your Monthly Budget, add a row for each outgoing category and set its Type: Fixed, Variable, Debt, Savings or Sinking fund. Enter a Planned amount for each one, using your earlier trackers:

- Fixed Expense Tracker for fixed rows
- Variable Expense Tracker for variable rows
- Debt Tracker for debt rows
- Savings and Emergency Fund Trackers for savings rows
- Sinking Fund Planner for sinking fund rows

Add one small buffer row.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Before this month begins, read your budget top to bottom once. For each row, ask: "Is this number realistic, based on what I actually spend?" Adjust any that are wishful. A plan you can follow beats a perfect plan you abandon by the second week.

questions.q: Where should the planned amount for groceries come from?
options: The lowest amount you can imagine
Your observed baseline from tracking actual spending
questions.explain: Starting from your real baseline keeps the budget achievable. You can reduce it gradually if you choose.

questions.q: Why include a small buffer row?
options: To catch small forgotten costs without breaking the plan
Because it is required by law
questions.explain: A buffer absorbs small surprises so the rest of the plan stays intact. It is not a replacement for an emergency fund.

sections.markdown:
- Every outgoing category has a type and a planned amount.
- Debt, savings and sinking funds are included, not left for "whatever is left".
- Your budget has a small buffer.

lessons.title: Calculate Remaining Money
lessons.summary: See exactly what is left after every planned expense and allocation.

sections.what: Remaining money is what is left after you subtract every planned expense, debt payment and savings allocation from income.
sections.why: This one number tells you whether the plan works before the month starts, not after.
sections.do: Use the Budget Calculator to work out your remaining amount, then decide what to do with it.
sections.output: Your remaining amount and a decision for it

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
The core calculation is:

> **Income − planned expenses − savings/debt allocations = remaining amount**

The goal is to understand the complete picture **before** spending.

The Budget Calculator shows every part of this calculation in its own column: income, fixed, variable, debt, savings and sinking funds. The remaining amount is income minus all of the others. Nothing is hidden.

There are three possible results:

1. **Positive remaining.** Money has no job yet. Decide on one: add to the buffer, an emergency fund, a sinking fund, a debt, or a planned treat. Unassigned money tends to disappear.
2. **Zero remaining.** Every unit of income has a job. Many people aim for this.
3. **Negative remaining.** Your plan needs more money than you expect to receive. This needs a decision before the month starts.

**If remaining is negative,** you can look at:

- Variable categories that could be reduced realistically
- Sinking fund target dates that could move later
- Fixed costs to review or renegotiate (from Module 3)
- Extra debt payments above the minimum that could pause for a month
- Whether any income was left out

Be careful about reducing minimum debt payments or essential costs. Missing required payments can have serious consequences. If you are struggling to cover essentials and minimums, consider speaking to your creditor or a reputable, independent debt or money advice service in your country.

A negative number is not a judgement. It is the plan telling you the truth early enough to act.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Musa enters his month in the Budget Calculator:

Income 18,000. Fixed 8,000. Variable 5,500. Debt 2,500. Savings 1,000. Sinking funds 1,500.

Remaining: 18,000 − 8,000 − 5,500 − 2,500 − 1,000 − 1,500 = −500.

He moves one sinking fund date later (saving 300 a month) and reduces his variable spending plan by 200. New remaining: 0. The plan now works on paper before the month starts.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Budget Calculator and add a row for this month:

1. Enter total planned income.
2. Enter your planned totals for fixed, variable, debt, savings and sinking funds from your Monthly Budget.
3. Read the Remaining column.
4. If positive, give the money a job. If negative, choose one or two adjustments and recalculate.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Before each new month, run the Budget Calculator once. Add a new row for each month so you can see how your remaining amount changes across 2026. If you notice it is negative month after month, that pattern is worth a deeper review of your fixed costs and income in your monthly review.

questions.q: Income is 12,000. Fixed 5,000, variable 3,000, debt 1,500, savings 1,000, sinking funds 1,000. What is the remaining amount?
Your remaining amount is positive. What is the most useful next step?
options: Give it a specific job, such as a fund, buffer or planned treat
Spend it on the first day
questions.explain: Money without a job tends to disappear. Assigning it keeps the plan complete.

sections.markdown:
- You know the remaining-amount calculation.
- You have calculated this month's remaining amount.
- You have either given positive money a job or adjusted a negative result.

lessons.title: Give Every Category a Review Rule
lessons.summary: Compare planned and actual amounts and decide what each difference means.

sections.what: A review rule is a simple habit for each category: compare planned with actual, note why they differ, and decide whether to adjust.
sections.why: Without a review, the same gap repeats every month. With one, your budget gets more accurate over time.
sections.do: Fill in actual amounts, read the difference, and add a reason and adjustment in Notes for any large gaps.
sections.output: A reviewed Monthly Budget with notes and adjustments

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
For every category in your budget, track five things:

- **Planned amount:** what you expected.
- **Actual amount:** what really happened.
- **Difference:** planned − actual. Calculated for you.
- **Reason for difference:** a few words in Notes.
- **Adjustment if needed:** what you will change next month.

**How to read the difference:**

- On **expense rows** (Fixed, Variable, Debt, Savings, Sinking fund): a positive difference means you spent or allocated less than planned. A negative difference means you went over.
- On **income rows**: it works the other way round. A positive difference means less income arrived than planned. A negative difference means more arrived.

**Set a simple rule for when to act.** For example: "If a category is off by more than about 10%, or by an amount that matters to me, I write a reason." Small differences are normal and do not need a story.

Common reasons and adjustments:

- **One-off event** (a birthday, a repair): no change, but consider a sinking fund next time.
- **Plan was unrealistic:** raise the planned amount and reduce another category.
- **Price increase:** update the planned amount from next month.
- **Unplanned habit:** decide whether to plan for it or reduce it.

The aim is not to prove you were "good". It is to make next month's plan more accurate.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
At month-end, Fatima's budget shows:

- Groceries: planned 3,000, actual 3,600, difference −600. Reason: hosted family twice. Adjustment: add a small hosting line to sinking funds.
- Transport: planned 1,500, actual 1,200, difference 300. Reason: worked from home more. Adjustment: none yet, watch one more month.
- Salary: planned 15,000, actual 15,000, difference 0.

Two notes, two decisions, ten minutes.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
For the current or most recent month:

1. Enter the actual amount for every row in your Monthly Budget.
2. Read the Difference column, remembering it reads differently for income rows.
3. For any category off by more than your rule, write the reason and adjustment in Notes.
4. Choose one adjustment to apply to next month's planned amounts.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Write your personal review rule in one sentence, for example: "Any category off by 10% or more gets a reason and an adjustment." At month-end, apply it to every row. Carry your adjustments into next month's budget before the month starts, so each budget builds on what you learned.

questions.q: On an expense row, planned is 2,000 and actual is 2,500. What does the difference of −500 mean?
questions.explain: Difference is planned − actual. A negative result on an expense row means you went over the plan.

questions.q: On an income row, planned is 10,000 and actual is 9,000. What does the difference of 1,000 mean?
questions.explain: On income rows a positive difference means less arrived than planned, so you may need to adjust spending.

sections.markdown:
- Every category has a planned and actual amount.
- You can read the difference correctly for income and expense rows.
- You have a personal review rule and at least one adjustment for next month.

modules.title: Weekly Money Check-In
modules.summary: A short, regular review that catches problems before the end of the month. You build a five-minute habit and a monthly review that keeps your plan current.
modules.outcome: Your Weekly Money Check-In and Monthly Money Review

lessons.title: Why Weekly?
lessons.summary: See how a short weekly review keeps your budget useful all month.

sections.what: A weekly money check-in is a short, scheduled review of your spending, upcoming bills and progress.
sections.why: Problems are easier to fix when they are small. A weekly look can catch an overspend in week two instead of discovering it on day thirty.
sections.do: Choose a fixed day, time and place for your weekly check-in.
sections.output: A scheduled weekly check-in slot

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A monthly budget is a plan. A month is a long time for a plan to run without checking in.

If you only review at month-end, you find out about problems when it is too late to change them. A **weekly check-in** gives you four or five chances a month to notice and adjust.

**What weekly reviews help with:**

- Catching a category that is running ahead of plan while there is still time to slow down
- Seeing bills that are due before the next payday
- Recording unexpected costs while you still remember what they were
- Keeping your trackers up to date, so month-end takes minutes, not hours

**What makes the habit stick:**

- **Same day, same time.** Many people choose a quiet evening or the morning after payday. Choose what suits your week.
- **Short.** Five to fifteen minutes. If it takes an hour, it will not last.
- **Attach it to something you already do,** such as a Sunday coffee or the evening you plan meals.
- **Keep the tools ready.** Your banking app, your Monthly Budget and the Weekly Money Check-In form.
- **No judgement.** The check-in is for information, not blame. If a week went badly, you write it down and adjust.

If you share finances with a partner or household, a joint weekly check-in can reduce surprises and arguments. Keep it short and practical.

Missing a week is normal. Just do the next one. The value comes from the pattern over time, not from never missing.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Before, Neo checked his bank balance only when he felt worried. Twice he went over his grocery plan without noticing until the last week.

Now he does a ten-minute check-in every Sunday after breakfast. In week two of March, he saw that groceries were already at 70% of plan. He planned simpler meals for the next week and finished the month on budget.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Decide and write down:

1. **Day** of the week for your check-in.
2. **Time** of day.
3. **Place** where you will do it.
4. **Trigger:** what you will attach it to (coffee, meal planning, payday).
5. **Tools:** banking app, Monthly Budget, Weekly Money Check-In form.

Add it to your phone calendar as a repeating event.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Do your first check-in this week, even if it is rough. Open your banking app and your Monthly Budget side by side for five minutes. Do not try to fix everything. Just look. Next week, use the full five-question check from the next lesson.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of a weekly check-in compared with only reviewing at month-end?
options: It guarantees you will never overspend
It lets you catch and adjust problems while there is still time in the month
It removes the need to track spending
questions.explain: Weekly reviews give several chances to adjust during the month. They do not guarantee outcomes.

questions.q: Which approach makes a weekly habit most likely to stick?
options: A long, detailed review whenever you remember
A short review on the same day and time each week
Reviewing only when you feel stressed
Waiting until you have more money
questions.explain: Short, predictable reviews are easier to keep up.

sections.markdown:
- You understand why a weekly review helps.
- You have chosen a day, time, place and trigger.
- Your check-in is in your calendar.

lessons.title: Five-Minute Money Check
lessons.summary: Use five simple questions to review your week in about five minutes.

sections.what: The Five-Minute Money Check is a set of five questions you answer each week.
sections.why: The same questions every week make the review quick, consistent and easy to compare over time.
sections.do: Answer the five questions in your Weekly Money Check-In form.
sections.output: Your first completed Weekly Money Check-In

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Each week, ask:

1. **What did I spend?** Look at your bank and card transactions for the week. Add up the main categories, or at least the total. Update the Actual column in your Monthly Budget for the main categories.
2. **What bills are coming?** Check the next 7 to 14 days. Use your Fixed Expense Tracker, Debt Tracker and Annual Expense Calendar. Is the money in the right account?
3. **Did anything unexpected happen?** A repair, a gift, a price increase, a missed payment. Write it down. If it is truly an emergency, it may come from your emergency fund. If it will happen again, it may need a sinking fund.
4. **Am I still on track?** Compare spending so far with your plan. A rough rule: about a quarter of the way through the month, variable categories might be around a quarter used. This is a guide, not a rule, because some spending happens in large weekly shops.
5. **What needs adjusting?** Choose one small change for the coming week, if any. For example, "Move 200 from entertainment to groceries" or "Pay the water bill on Tuesday."

**Keep answers short.** A number and one sentence per question is enough.

**One action is enough.** The check-in is not a moment to rebuild your whole budget. Choose the single most useful adjustment and do it.

If you see a bigger problem, such as income being much lower than expected, note it and bring it to your monthly review, where you have time to rethink properly.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Amahle's check-in, week two of May:

1. Spent: 2,100. Groceries 1,200, transport 400, eating out 500.
2. Bills coming: electricity on the 15th, phone on the 18th. Money is in the account.
3. Unexpected: 300 for a school trip.
4. On track? Eating out is at 80% of plan halfway through the month.
5. Adjust: no more eating out this week; move 300 from buffer to cover the school trip.

Time taken: six minutes.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Weekly Money Check-In form and complete it for this week:

1. Enter the date.
2. Answer each of the five questions with a number and a short sentence.
3. Choose whether you are on track.
4. Write one adjustment for next week.
5. Rate how in control you feel, from 1 to 5. Over time this shows your progress.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Use the form every week at your scheduled time. Save each check-in so you can look back at the month during your monthly review. After four weeks, read them together: patterns such as the same category running over every week will stand out clearly.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the five check-in questions?
questions.explain: The five questions cover spending, upcoming bills, surprises, progress and adjustments. Investment choices are outside this check-in.

questions.q: Your check-in shows income for the month will be much lower than planned. What is the best approach?
options: Make a small adjustment now and bring the bigger rethink to your monthly review
Rebuild your whole system during the five-minute check
questions.explain: The weekly check-in handles quick adjustments. Bigger changes deserve the time of a monthly review.

sections.markdown:
- You know the five questions.
- You have completed your first Weekly Money Check-In.
- You have one adjustment for the coming week.

lessons.title: Make Adjustments
lessons.summary: Update your plan calmly as new information arrives, weekly and monthly.

sections.what: Making adjustments means changing future planned amounts based on what actually happened, without abandoning the budget.
sections.why: A budget is a plan, not a punishment. Plans that adjust survive real life; rigid ones get dropped.
sections.do: Complete a Monthly Money Review and record the adjustments for next month.
sections.output: Your first Monthly Money Review

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
> A budget is a plan, not a punishment.

Real life will not match your plan exactly. Prices rise, people get sick, cars break, income shifts. The point of reviewing is to **update future spending based on current information.**

**Weekly adjustments** are small and quick:

- Move money between flexible categories (for example, from entertainment to groceries)
- Pause a non-essential purchase until next month
- Use the buffer for a small surprise

**Monthly adjustments** are more considered. Once a month, use the Monthly Money Review to:

- Compare total income and total spending with the plan
- Check savings, emergency fund and sinking fund progress
- Note the biggest difference and its reason
- Decide what worked and what did not
- Set planned amounts for next month

**Good adjustment habits:**

- **Move money, do not just overspend.** If a category goes over, decide which other category gives way. This keeps the plan balanced.
- **Separate one-offs from patterns.** A single expensive week is different from three months running over.
- **Protect essentials and required payments first.** Adjust flexible categories before essentials and minimum debt payments.
- **Write it down.** A one-line note today saves confusion later.

If adjustments are not enough, for example if essentials and minimum payments are consistently more than your income, it may be time to get help from a reputable, independent money or debt advice service in your country.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
At her June review, Busi sees that her transport spending was over plan three months in a row because of a fare increase. That is a pattern, not a one-off.

She raises transport by 400 for July, reduces clothing by 250 and entertainment by 150. Her plan now reflects reality. She notes the change in her Monthly Money Review, so she remembers why next time.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Monthly Money Review for your most recent month:

1. Enter actual income and actual total spending.
2. Record savings, debt payments and sinking fund contributions made.
3. Note the category with the biggest difference and why.
4. Write what worked and what was hard.
5. Choose up to three adjustments for next month.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Choose a monthly review date, such as the last weekend of each month or the day after payday, and put it in your calendar. Bring your weekly check-ins with you. Each review ends with next month's Monthly Budget updated. That is your system staying current.

questions.q: Your entertainment category is 300 over plan mid-month. What is a balanced adjustment?
options: Move 300 from another flexible category so the plan stays balanced
questions.explain: Moving money between flexible categories keeps the plan whole. Skipping required payments can cause serious problems.

questions.q: Transport has gone over plan for three months because fares increased. What does that suggest?
options: A pattern that calls for updating the planned amount
That you should stop tracking transport
questions.explain: Repeated differences signal that the plan needs updating to match reality.

sections.markdown:
- You know the difference between weekly and monthly adjustments.
- You have completed a Monthly Money Review.
- You have up to three adjustments for next month's budget.

modules.title: Annual Financial Planning
modules.summary: Look beyond one month and map the whole of 2026: bills, events, goals and income changes. You stop being surprised by costs that arrive once a year.
modules.outcome: Your 2026 Annual Financial Planner and Annual Expense Calendar

lessons.title: Look Beyond One Month
lessons.summary: Gather every known annual cost, event and goal for 2026 in one planner.

sections.what: Annual planning means listing the costs, income changes and goals that will affect your money across the whole year.
sections.why: Monthly budgets miss things that happen once or twice a year. Seeing the full year early gives you time to prepare.
sections.do: Complete your Annual Financial Planner with every known 2026 event, cost and goal.
sections.output: A completed 2026 Annual Financial Planner

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A monthly budget handles the next few weeks. Many of the costs that strain a budget do not happen monthly. Annual planning brings them into view.

List everything you know or expect for 2026 in eight areas:

- **Annual bills:** licences, memberships, annual subscriptions, domain names, professional fees.
- **Holidays:** festive season, family events, travel, school holidays.
- **Insurance:** renewal dates and any expected premium changes.
- **Major purchases:** furniture, appliances, a phone or laptop, a car.
- **Education expenses:** fees, uniforms, books, courses for you or your family.
- **Expected income changes:** a raise, a bonus, a contract ending, parental leave, a seasonal dip.
- **Savings goals:** emergency fund milestones, sinking funds, other targets.
- **Debt goals:** a debt you aim to clear or reduce by a certain date.

**Where to find them:** last year's bank statements, your email (search "renewal" or "invoice"), your calendar, school letters, and your Financial Goals Planner from Module 8.

**Estimate when you do not know.** A rough amount is much better than nothing. Mark it as an estimate and update it when you get a real quote.

**Tax and legal events** such as tax filing dates or provisional payments vary by country and personal situation. If they apply to you, check dates and amounts with your country's official tax authority or a qualified adviser rather than relying on general guides.

This list is not a promise to spend. It is a map of what is likely to come, so nothing arrives as a surprise.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Sipho spends 20 minutes going through last year's bank statements and email. He finds:

- Car licence renewal (March, about 600)
- Home insurance renewal (July, increase expected)
- School fees and uniforms (January, about 5,000)
- Family wedding (September, travel about 3,000)
- Contract bonus (December, not guaranteed)

Five events he would otherwise have met as surprises.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Annual Financial Planner and fill in each section. Use lists for multiple items. For each item, add a rough amount and month if you can. Then choose your top three financial priorities for 2026.

Do not aim for perfect. Aim for complete enough that the big things are visible.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: This week, search your email and last year's statements for the words "annual", "renewal" and "yearly". Add anything you find to your Annual Financial Planner. Keep the planner open during your monthly reviews so new items get added as soon as you hear about them.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in your annual plan rather than only your monthly budget?
options: A licence renewal due once a year in March
questions.explain: Annual costs are easy to miss in a monthly budget. The annual plan brings them into view early.

questions.q: You are unsure how a tax deadline applies to your situation. What should you do?
options: Check with your country's official tax authority or a qualified adviser
questions.explain: Tax rules vary by country and situation, so verify with an official or qualified source.

sections.markdown:
- You have listed annual bills, holidays, insurance, purchases and education costs.
- You have noted expected income changes, savings goals and debt goals.
- You have chosen your top three priorities for 2026.

lessons.title: Create the Annual Calendar
lessons.summary: Place every major expense and income event on a month-by-month 2026 calendar.

sections.what: The Annual Expense Calendar places each major cost and income event in the month it is expected.
sections.why: Seeing the year month by month shows heavy months in advance, so you can spread the load with sinking funds.
sections.do: Enter each item from your Annual Financial Planner into the calendar with its month, type and amount.
sections.output: A 2026 Annual Expense Calendar

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Your Annual Financial Planner is a list. The **Annual Expense Calendar** puts it on a timeline.

For each item, record:

- **Month:** when the cost is due or the income change happens.
- **Item:** a short name, such as "Car licence".
- **Type:** Annual bill, Holiday, Insurance, Major purchase, Education, Income change, Savings goal or Debt goal.
- **Amount:** the estimated or known amount.
- **Set aside:** tick this once the money for the item is ready, usually in a sinking fund.

**Look for heavy months.** Once the calendar is filled in, scan month by month. Many people find two or three months carry most of the irregular costs, often around the start of the year and the festive season. These are the months that used to feel like crises.

**Spread the load.** For each large item, check that it has a sinking fund in your Sinking Fund Planner. If not, add one. The earlier you start, the smaller the monthly contribution.

**Line up income events.** If you expect a bonus, a tax refund or a seasonal rise in income, note it, but treat it as uncertain until it arrives. Avoid planning a large cost that only works if uncertain income turns up.

**Note on the total:** the calendar adds up every amount you enter. If you include income changes, remember they are not costs, so read the total with that in mind or keep income rows separate in your review.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Lindiwe fills in her calendar and sees that January has school fees (5,000), a car service (2,000) and an insurance premium increase. December has gifts (3,000) and travel (4,000). Those two months hold 14,000 of costs.

She checks her Sinking Fund Planner: school fees and gifts are covered, but the car service and travel are not. She adds them. Next January will still be expensive, but it will be planned.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Annual Expense Calendar. For each item in your Annual Financial Planner:

1. Choose the month.
2. Enter the item name.
3. Choose the type.
4. Enter the amount.
5. Tick Set aside if the money is already saved.

Then scan for your two heaviest months and check every large item there has a sinking fund.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Copy the items for the next three months into your phone calendar, a week or two before each one is due, with the amount in the reminder. That gives you time to check the money is ready. Each month, look at the next quarter on your Annual Expense Calendar during your monthly review.

questions.q: You notice January and December carry most of your irregular costs. What is a sensible response?
options: Hope those months are better this year
Set up sinking funds early so those costs are spread across the year
Use the emergency fund every January
questions.explain: Sinking funds spread predictable costs across the year, which is exactly what heavy months need.

questions.q: What does the Set aside tick mean in the calendar?
options: The money for this item is already saved and ready
questions.explain: Ticking Set aside shows the cost is already covered, so you can see at a glance what still needs funding.

sections.markdown:
- Every known 2026 item is on your Annual Expense Calendar.
- You have identified your heaviest months.
- Large items in those months have sinking funds.

lessons.title: Monthly Review of the Annual Plan
lessons.summary: Keep your annual plan current with a short update at each month-end.

sections.what: This is a short month-end routine to update your annual plan with what happened and what has changed.
sections.why: An annual plan made in January will be out of date by March unless it is updated. A few minutes a month keeps it reliable.
sections.do: At month-end, update actuals, move completed goals, adjust targets and add new known expenses.
sections.output: An up-to-date annual plan and a month-end routine

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
At each month-end, as part of your Monthly Money Review, spend five to ten minutes on your annual plan. Use four steps:

1. **Update actuals.** For items due this month, replace estimates with the real amount paid or received. Tick Set aside for items that are now funded.
2. **Move completed goals.** If a goal is done, such as a sinking fund that has been spent or a debt that is paid off, mark it complete. Reset repeating items for next year if needed. Notice what you finished. It matters.
3. **Adjust upcoming targets.** If a price has gone up, a date has moved, or your income has changed, update the amounts and dates. Then update the Sinking Fund Planner so the suggested contributions stay accurate.
4. **Add new known expenses.** A new invitation, a school notice, an insurance letter. Add it now while you remember.

**Look three months ahead.** After updating, read the next three months on your calendar. Is everything there either funded or on track? If something is not, decide now: increase a contribution, move a date, or reduce the amount.

**Once a year, do a bigger annual review.** Pick a month, often near the end or start of the year. Look at the whole year: what you planned, what happened, what you learned. Then build the next year's plan using the same planner and calendar.

The annual plan works because it is updated, not because it was perfect on day one.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
At the end of April, Karabo updates her annual plan:

- Actuals: car licence cost 650, not 600. Updated.
- Completed: Easter travel fund spent, marked done.
- Adjust: insurance renewal in July is expected to rise. She raises the target from 2,400 to 2,700 and updates the sinking fund.
- New: friend's wedding in August, about 1,500. Added.

Then she reads May to July. Everything is funded or on track. Eight minutes.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Run the four steps for the month that just ended:

1. Update actuals on your Annual Expense Calendar.
2. Mark completed goals in your Annual Financial Planner.
3. Adjust any upcoming targets and update your Sinking Fund Planner.
4. Add any new known expenses.

Then read the next three months and note anything not yet funded.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Add "annual plan update" as the final step of your Monthly Money Review so it happens every month. Choose a month for your bigger annual review and put it in your calendar now. You will record this in your Money OS Builder in Module 12.

questions.q: Which is one of the four month-end steps for the annual plan?
questions.explain: The four steps are update actuals, move completed goals, adjust upcoming targets and add new known expenses.

questions.q: Your insurance renewal is expected to rise. What should you update besides the annual calendar?
options: Your Sinking Fund Planner target, so the suggested contribution stays accurate
questions.explain: Updating the sinking fund target keeps the monthly contribution realistic for the new amount.

sections.markdown:
- You know the four month-end steps.
- You have updated your annual plan for the month just ended.
- You have chosen a month for your bigger annual review.

modules.title: Build Your 2026 Money OS
modules.summary: Combine everything you have built into one connected system with a clear review rhythm. You leave with your 2026 Money OS and a plan to keep it running.

lessons.title: The 369 Money Loop
lessons.summary: See how every part of your system connects in one repeating loop.

sections.what: The 369 Money Loop is the order in which your money system flows and repeats: Income, Expenses, Budget, Savings, Debt, Goals, Weekly Review, Monthly Review, Annual Review.
sections.why: Seeing the loop shows how each tool feeds the next, so a change in one place is carried through the whole system.
sections.do: Trace one recent change in your finances through each step of the loop.
sections.output: A clear picture of how your system connects

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Over eleven modules you have built separate tools. The **369 Money Loop** shows how they work together:

> **Income → Expenses → Budget → Savings → Debt → Goals → Weekly Review → Monthly Review → Annual Review**

- **Income:** what you expect to receive, and when.
- **Expenses:** fixed commitments and variable spending patterns.
- **Budget:** income allocated to every expense and goal, with a clear remaining amount.
- **Savings:** your emergency fund and other savings with targets.
- **Debt:** every balance, payment and your chosen repayment approach.
- **Goals:** sinking funds and bigger goals with contributions and dates.
- **Weekly Review:** five questions, one adjustment.
- **Monthly Review:** planned versus actual, adjustments, next month's budget.
- **Annual Review:** the full year, heavy months, and next year's plan.

**It is a loop, not a line.** Each review feeds back into the start. A weekly check-in may show a new cost, which updates your expenses, which changes your budget. A monthly review may show income has changed, which flows through everything after it.

**The core philosophy is Visibility → Planning → Control → Review.** You see clearly, plan ahead, make choices with information, and review so the system stays current.

The objective is not perfection. It is **visibility and repeatable decision-making.** Some months will go to plan; others will not. The loop is how you recover without starting over.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Joseph's phone contract goes up by 100 a month.

- **Expenses:** he updates his Fixed Expense Tracker.
- **Budget:** his remaining amount drops by 100. He reduces entertainment by 100.
- **Savings, Debt, Goals:** unchanged, protected by the adjustment.
- **Weekly Review:** he checks the new amount was debited correctly.
- **Monthly Review:** he notes the change and reason.
- **Annual Review:** he adds "review phone contract" to his November plan.

One change, handled calmly through the whole loop.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Think of one change in your finances from the last three months: a price increase, a new expense, a change in income, or a goal reached.

Write down how it affects each step of the loop: Income, Expenses, Budget, Savings, Debt, Goals, Weekly Review, Monthly Review, Annual Review. If it does not affect a step, write "no change". Then note which tool you need to update.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown: Over the next week, whenever something changes, such as a new bill, an unexpected cost or extra income, ask yourself: "Where does this enter the loop, and what does it change downstream?" Update the first tool, then follow the loop. Your next Monthly Money Review is a good time to check that every tool reflects the change.

sections.what: Your 2026 Money OS is your complete system: eleven connected tools plus your review schedule, money rules and next actions.

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Your final build brings together eleven parts:

1. **Financial Snapshot:** your starting point.
2. **Income system:** Income Tracker and calendar.
3. **Fixed expense tracker:** every recurring commitment.
4. **Variable expense tracker:** your real spending patterns.
5. **Debt dashboard:** every debt and your chosen approach.
6. **Savings system:** savings goals with targets.
7. **Emergency fund plan:** your target, milestone and tracker.
8. **Sinking funds:** planned irregular costs with contributions.
9. **Monthly budget:** planned, actual and difference for every category.
10. **Weekly review:** your five-minute check-in.
11. **Annual plan:** your 2026 planner and calendar.

The **Money OS Builder** pulls in what you have saved in each of these tools, so you can see the whole system on one screen.

**Then you add three things that make it yours:**

- **Review schedule:** your weekly check-in day, monthly review date and annual review month.
- **Money rules:** short personal rules that guide decisions. For example: "Every unit of income gets a job before the month starts." "I use the three-question test before touching the emergency fund." "If a category is over by 10%, I write a reason." "New annual costs go on the calendar the day I hear about them."
- **Next actions:** the specific things still to do, such as "Set up transfer for sinking funds" or "Get insurance quote by March".

Keep money rules few, short and in your own words. Three to five is plenty. They should describe how you want to make decisions, not targets you must hit.

If any part is still empty, that is fine. Add it to your next actions. A system that is 80% complete and in use is far more valuable than one waiting to be perfect.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Rethabile opens the Money OS Builder. Nine parts are complete. Her variable expense tracker has only two weeks of data, and her annual calendar is missing the second half of the year.

She sets her schedule: check-in Sunday, monthly review on the 26th, annual review in November. Her rules: "Plan before payday." "Emergencies only pass the three-question test." "Move money, do not just overspend." Her next actions: finish tracking variable spending for two more weeks and complete July to December on the calendar.

sections.what: Keeping it running means checking your Money OS meets the completion criteria, following your review schedule, and using the 7-Day Money Reset when life gets in the way.
sections.why: Every system drifts. A clear standard and a simple way back mean a missed month is a pause, not the end.

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
**Completion criteria.** Your 2026 Money OS is built when you can see:

- Expected income
- Planned expenses
- Savings targets
- Debt obligations
- Upcoming irregular expenses
- Current financial goals
- Your weekly and monthly review process

If you can answer "where is that?" for each one in under a minute, your system is working.

**Your review schedule.**

- **Weekly (5 to 15 minutes):** the five-question check-in and one adjustment.
- **Monthly (30 to 60 minutes):** the Monthly Money Review, update the annual plan, build next month's budget.
- **Annually (1 to 2 hours):** review the year, update your emergency-fund target and goals, and build next year's plan and calendar.

**The 7-Day Money Reset.** If you fall off for a few weeks or months, do not start from scratch. Spend 15 to 30 minutes a day for a week:

1. **Day 1:** Financial snapshot. Update your current position.
2. **Day 2:** Income. Confirm what is coming in and when.
3. **Day 3:** Fixed expenses. Check what has changed.
4. **Day 4:** Variable spending. Look at the last few weeks.
5. **Day 5:** Debt and savings. Update balances.
6. **Day 6:** Goals and sinking funds. Adjust targets and dates.
7. **Day 7:** Build your monthly budget.

Then return to your weekly check-ins.

Remember: this system is general budgeting and organisation education. For decisions about investments, tax, legal matters or credit, check current information with an official source or a qualified, independent adviser in your country.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
After a busy few months, Lwazi had not opened his budget since April. In July he did the 7-Day Money Reset, about 20 minutes each evening.

By day 7 he had an updated snapshot, two new expenses added, a sinking fund date moved, and a July budget built. The following Sunday he did his first check-in in three months. No restart, just a reset.
